absurdist.claim: Absurdist drama, Beckett above all, asks actors for exact control of timing, rhythm and timed silence, and in Waiting for Godot for the cross-talk and clown business of vaudeville and music hall.
absurdist.source: State Theatre Company South Australia, 'Beckett Trip' study guide, https://statetheatrecompany.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Beckett-study-guide.pdf; Wikipedia, 'Waiting for Godot' (pointer only), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waiting_for_Godot; Northern Star, 'Beckett: Double acts, music hall and his relationship to theatre', https://northernstarcr.wordpress.com/2015/12/15/beckett-double-acts-music-hall-and-his-relationship-to-theatre/
absurdist.sourceSupports: The study guide, from a search summary: Beckett 'places strong emphasis on the rhythmic qualities of his plays, and like a composer, he is conscious of the importance of precisely timed silence'; his plays put actors in very difficult positions, some unable to speak and others unable to move; one actress says the voice must concentrate on 'timing, rhythm and the musicality of the text'. Wikipedia, from a search summary, says Godot borrows from 'the cross-talk tradition of the vaudeville stage, the burlesque, the music hall, and the movies of Charlie Chaplin, Buster Keaton, Laurel and Hardy', with hat games, dropped trousers and similar business. The Northern Star blog says Godot owes much of its form and rhythm to vaudeville and clown acts.

tags.why: The study guide stresses timing, rhythm and precisely timed silence; the Godot sources describe vaudeville cross-talk. That is comic timing, though it is shown for Beckett, not for every absurdist author.
The Godot sources name clown and music-hall acts, Laurel and Hardy hat games and dropped trousers as part of the play’s humor. This is shown for Godot only.

absurdist.uncertainty: All of the evidence is Beckett, mostly Godot. Ionesco, Pinter and absurdist film aren’t covered. The study guide’s PDF couldn’t be read as text, so the quotations come from a search engine’s summary of it, not from a direct reading. No source found covers 'holding comedy and despair together' as an acting demand in so many words. On review (October 10, 2026), evidence that’s all Beckett wasn’t enough to make it a requirement of the whole genre.
absurdist.belongsTo: Beckett’s plays (Waiting for Godot’s cross-talk and clown business)

adventure.claim: A film reference work treats action and adventure cinema together as a form that foregrounds the body in motion and in combat, with a hero who must show physical endurance. In its swashbuckler strand the hero displays martial skill in extravagant swordplay, and stars such as Fairbanks did much of their own stunt work.
adventure.source: Yvonne Tasker, Action and Adventure Films (Schirmer Encyclopedia of Film (ed. Barry Keith Grant), via Encyclopedia.com, 2007), https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/action-and-adventure-films [read directly]; Wisconsin Center for Film and Theater Research (blog post), Douglas Fairbanks: No Stuntman Required (WCFTR, University of Wisconsin-Madison, 2013), https://wcftr.commarts.wisc.edu/index.php/2013/05/16/douglas-fairbanks-no-stuntman-required/ [read directly]; Jeffrey Richards, Swordsmen of the Screen: From Douglas Fairbanks to Michael York (Routledge & Kegan Paul (reissued Routledge 2014), 1977), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swashbuckler_film [from a search summary]
adventure.sourceSupports: Action and Adventure Films: "as a form that foregrounds the body in motion and in combat, action and adventure cinema advances a physical (frequently sexualized), imagery of heroism"; "the action or adventure hero is called upon to demonstrate courage, initiative and physical endurance"; the swashbuckler hero is shown "displaying martial skills in extravagant scenes of swordplay"; Flynn’s "athletic performance came to define the romantic male exuberance of the swashbuckler." Douglas Fairbanks: No Stuntman Required: Fairbanks "completed most stunts himself" and secretly did the Robin Hood drawbridge stunt after agreeing to a double. It makes no claim about swashbuckler stars in general. Swordsmen of the Screen: From Douglas Fairbanks to Michael York: Quoted (via Wikipedia, not read directly) as saying that to understand a swashbuckler 'we must look at the art director, costume designer, fencing master, stunt arranger, cinematographer and actor'. The book’s existence and authorship are confirmed by the Wikipedia citation; the quote itself wasn’t seen on a page read directly.
adventure.how: two of its three sources read directly and the remaining one from a search summary, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: Tasker’s encyclopedia entry says of the whole form that action and adventure cinema foregrounds the body in motion and in combat, which makes on-screen combat a convention of the genre. It’s one credible source, so the research holds it at medium confidence, not high. Stars doing their own stunts (Fairbanks, Flynn) is a matter for swashbuckler stars, and isn’t what the requirement rests on.

adventure.uncertainty: Tasker treats action and adventure as one form; scholars such as Brian Taves separate historical adventure from action, and some adventure films (travel or exploration stories) have little combat. Only one source says it of the whole genre directly. The Richards quote wasn’t read in the book itself.

alternate_history.claim: No source was found that describes a performance demand particular to alternate history.
alternate_history.source: None found. A search for actors' approach on The Man in the High Castle returned only cast lists and low-quality pages
alternate_history.sourceSupports: The search found nothing usable. One page it found (explore.st-aug.edu) was generic, unsourced text, and wasn’t used.
alternate_history.uncertainty: The genre is defined by its premise, not its performance, and its definition calls for none of the requirements the game can ask for. Anything a period asks would come from the period the story imitates, which the Costume Drama genre covers, not from this one.

animated.claim: Actors in animation perform with the voice alone, usually alone in a recording booth and often before the animation exists, putting a full physical performance into what is only heard.
animated.source: Backstage, 'How to Become a Cartoon Voice Actor', https://www.backstage.com/magazine/article/how-to-become-a-voice-actor-cartoons-75311/; Real Voice Talent, 'Voice Acting for Animation: Different Skills Required for Character Voices', https://www.realvotalent.com/blog/voice-acting-for-animation-different-skills-required-for-character-voices
animated.sourceSupports: From a search summary: 'Voice actors may or may not have a scene partner while recording, so they practice delivering their dialogue solo'; voice actors 'stand alone in a soundproof room while delivering a full-body performance that audiences will only ever hear'; the best animation voice actors 'gesture, crouch, jump, and grimace while recording'. A further result (a TikTok video, not used as a source) described prelay, recording before animation. The summary merged several pages, so which page holds which sentence wasn’t checked.

tags.why: The sources describe the animation actor’s job as voice-only performance in a booth, often without a scene partner.

animated.uncertainty: Neither page was read directly. The claim is widely repeated, but repetition wasn’t counted as extra support. Stop-motion and motion-capture work differ and aren’t covered.

anime.claim: Dubbing anime asks the actor to match timing to mouth movements that already exist, keeping the performance emotionally true while it fits the lip flaps.
anime.source: D.C. Douglas, 'Tips For ADR Voice Acting in Anime Dubbing', https://dcdouglas.com/voiceover-resources/adr-dubbing-voice-acting/; Mix, 'The Art of Anime Dubbing', https://www.mixonline.com/sfp/art-anime-dubbing-369119
anime.sourceSupports: D.C. Douglas (read directly) quotes voice actors. Crispin Freeman: 'It’s like a dance where timing is everything. Practicing with the lip flaps in silent mode can help you get the timing down.' Cherami Leigh: 'focus on matching the mouth movements precisely.' Mary Elizabeth McGlynn: 'You need to feel what the character feels.' Mix (from a search summary): the hardest problem for dubbing directors is 'getting natural performances from actors who are trying to match the rhythms of pre-existing mouth flaps'.

tags.why: Both sources describe voice-only performance synced to existing animation.

anime.uncertainty: This covers English-language dubbing only. The original Japanese voice performance (seiyuu work) wasn’t researched. A 'heightened, expressive register' isn’t supported by anything found.

anthology.claim: Some anthology films cast one actor in several roles across their stories, but no source treats this as a convention of the form.
anthology.source: Wikipedia, 'List of actors who have played multiple roles in the same film' (pointer only), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_actors_who_have_played_multiple_roles_in_the_same_film; Collider, '13 Best Movies With Actors Playing Multiple Roles', https://collider.com/best-movies-actors-play-multiple-roles-austin-powers/
anthology.sourceSupports: From a search summary, examples only: Cloud Atlas, where the cast play multiple roles across eras; Gene Kelly in different characters in each story of Invitation to the Dance; Mel Brooks in four roles in History of the World, Part I.
anthology.uncertainty: These are examples, not a convention, and nothing found supports 'establishing a character quickly in a short segment'. Cloud Atlas also shows heavy makeup transformation, but that’s one film, so the research doesn’t name Physical Transformation for the genre.

apocalyptic.claim: Only a single example was found: on The Road, the lead lost about 30 pounds and lived rough to play a starving survivor.
apocalyptic.source: Collider, 'Viggo Mortensen Interview THE ROAD', https://collider.com/viggo-mortensen-interview-the-road/; Daily Actor, 'Viggo Mortensen on The Road and Preparation for His Role', https://www.dailyactor.com/actors-on-acting/viggo-mortensen-on-the-road-and-preparation-for-his-role/
apocalyptic.sourceSupports: From a search summary: Mortensen lost around 30 pounds by eating less; he 'literally became weaker'; he said the weight loss was the hardest part; some of the cast went days without showering.
apocalyptic.uncertainty: This is one film. Physical transformation is shown there but not established as a convention of the genre, so the research doesn’t name Physical Transformation. 'Sustained fear, grief and desperation played truthfully' isn’t supported by any source found.

art_house.claim: In the modernist strand of art cinema (Bresson, Antonioni), directors hold actors’ physical and vocal expressivity so far down that framing, editing and sound carry the characters’ inner life. Bresson called his performers 'models', not actors, and repeated lines until the 'acting' was gone.
art_house.source: Cynthia Baron, Acting (Schirmer Encyclopedia of Film, ed. Barry Keith Grant (Schirmer Reference/Thomson Gale), via Encyclopedia.com, 2007), https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/acting [read directly]; Tom Ryall, Art Cinema (Schirmer Encyclopedia of Film, via Encyclopedia.com, 2007), https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/art-cinema [read directly]; Donato Totaro, "Notes" on Notes on the Cinematographer (Offscreen, 2004), https://offscreen.com/view/bresson_notes [read directly]; David Bordwell, The Art Cinema as a Mode of Film Practice (Film Criticism 4:1, 1979), http://hybridstyle.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/04/Bordwell-The-Art-Cinema-as-a-Mode-of-Film-Practice.pdf [from a search summary]
art_house.sourceSupports: Acting: In modernist films by Bresson and Antonioni, 'actors' use of their physical and vocal expressivity is so delimited by the directors that glimpses of their characters' inner experiences often are more clearly conveyed by the directors' framing, editing, sound, and production design choices.' Also: 'The scale and quality of actors' physical and vocal expressions are also keyed to the film’s style or genre.' Art Cinema: It says nothing about an acting method for art cinema as a whole; only that 'art films tended to delve into character psychology and sensibility, to investigate the drama of the interior'. This is evidence against an acting convention for the whole genre. "Notes" on Notes on the Cinematographer: The Bressonian 'model' differs from an actor and 'encompasses an attitude ... which goes beyond performance'; repetition of lines is Bresson’s way of 'recovering the automatism of real life' (quoting Bresson, Notes on the Cinematographer, p. 59). The Art Cinema as a Mode of Film Practice: Art cinema motivates its narratives by realism and authorial expressivity and uses 'realistic', psychologically complex characters. It describes characters and narration, not an acting technique.
art_house.how: three of its four sources read directly and the remaining one from a search summary, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: subgenre-or-role: The restrained, minimal playing is documented for modernist directors (Bresson, Antonioni) and, in Bresson’s case, is explicitly anti-acting rather than naturalistic on-camera technique. The reference entry on art cinema itself names no acting convention, so it must not be applied to all art-house film.

art_house.uncertainty: Art house is a market and exhibition category covering many styles. Bresson’s book wasn’t read directly, only quoted through Totaro. Naturalism On Camera is only an approximation: Bresson’s models are closer to the absence of performance than to naturalistic screen acting.
art_house.belongsTo: the methods of particular modernist and auteur directors (Bresson, Antonioni) and of slow cinema

avant_garde.claim: No source on performing in avant-garde film was found. Sources on experimental theater (Grotowski) describe intensive physical and vocal actor training in place of naturalistic representation.
avant_garde.source: OCR, 'Topic Exploration Pack, Practitioners: Grotowski', https://coleshill.warwickshire.sch.uk/files/2020/07/299992-practitioners-grotowski.pdf; Jerzy Grotowski method page, https://www.dramaclasses.biz/jerzy-grotowski
avant_garde.sourceSupports: From a search summary: Grotowski 'was more interested in form' than in naturalistic portrayal of real life; his training integrated 'the physical, vocal, mental, emotional, and energetic lives of the actor'; he drew on Meyerhold’s biomechanics, Peking opera, kathakali and Nō.
avant_garde.uncertainty: The game defines the genre as film, and the sources are about experimental theater. Avant-garde film often has no actors at all, so nothing supports a requirement for the film genre. Movement-based work is plausible, but here it’s supported only for one theater practitioner.

biker.claim: On The Wild Angels (1966), the film usually credited with starting the cycle, Corman required the professional actors to do their own motorcycle riding, and a lead who couldn’t ride was replaced.
biker.source: TCM, 'The Wild Angels', https://www.tcm.com/articles/220878/the-wild-angels; Wikipedia, 'The Wild Angels' (pointer only), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wild_Angels
biker.sourceSupports: From a search summary: 'Corman insisted that all the professional actors had to ride the bikes themselves because he wanted to be as authentic as possible. The principals are clearly seen doing all their own riding'. Also: 'since Chakiris didn’t know how to ride a motorcycle, however, and refused to do the film without doubles and stuntmen, Corman then offered the role to Peter Fonda'. The TCM page couldn’t be opened.

tags.why: The source treats the riding as work that would otherwise go to doubles and stuntmen, and says the actors had to do it themselves. Shown for one founding film.

biker.uncertainty: This is one film’s casting rule, not a documented convention of the whole cycle. Riding fits Fights And Stunts only loosely, since none of the requirements the game can ask for is driving or riding. On review (October 10, 2026), one film’s casting rule wasn’t enough to make it a requirement of the whole genre.
biker.belongsTo: productions that ask actors to ride, as The Wild Angels did

biographical.claim: Playing a real person means working within documented fact: researching the subject and reproducing their voice, accent, mannerisms and movement, while trying to portray rather than impersonate.
biographical.source: Michelle Sabato, 'Acting In A Biographical Film: Playing The Real Part', Film Inquiry, https://www.filminquiry.com/acting-biographical-film/; Casting Networks, 'Breaking Into Biopics: How to Audition for Real-Life Roles', https://www.castingnetworks.com/news/breaking-into-biopics-how-to-audition-for-real-life-roles/
biographical.sourceSupports: Sabato (read directly): 'There is a fine line between portraying a person and impersonating a person.' Streep approached Thatcher’s voice like learning a song and worked with voice coaches on accent; Downey watched all of Chaplin’s films to reproduce his movement; Day-Lewis read over a hundred books on Lincoln to understand his physicality and speech. Biographical roles require working 'within the confines ... of an actual person’s existence'. Casting Networks (from a search summary): actors study footage, 'listening to their voice and observing their physicality'.

tags.why: The source describes reproducing a real person’s movement, physicality and mannerisms (Chaplin, Lincoln).

biographical.uncertainty: Film Inquiry is an independent film-criticism site, not a primary source. The examples are celebrated star performances, and not every biopic asks this much. The review of October 10, 2026 took Accents away: an accent is asked only where the subject spoke differently from the actor, which belongs to the role, not the genre.

black_comedy.claim: Reference works define black comedy as comedy that sets morbid or ghastly material against the comic, often through farce and low comedy. No credible source found states a specific acting technique (such as deadpan) for the genre; deadpan advice exists only for comedy in general.
black_comedy.source: The Editors of Encyclopaedia Britannica, Black humour (Encyclopaedia Britannica), https://www.britannica.com/topic/black-humor [from a search summary]; Richard Sheposh, Black comedy (EBSCO Research Starters, 2022), https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/social-sciences-and-humanities/black-comedy/ [read directly]; Vancouver Film School, Deadpan (VFS News, 2026), https://vfs.edu/news/deadpan [read directly]
black_comedy.sourceSupports: Black humor: Black humor is writing that juxtaposes morbid or ghastly elements with comical ones; it 'often uses farce and low comedy'. (The page couldn’t be opened, so this is from a search summary.) It defines the genre as comic and says nothing about acting. Black comedy: It treats black comedy as a form of comedy with film examples (Dr. Strangelove, Harold and Maude, Fargo, The Death of Stalin). It doesn’t discuss performance, deadpan or timing. Deadpan: It advises sincere commitment to absurd situations ('The more absurd the situation becomes, the more useful sincere commitment can be'). It doesn’t mention black or dark comedy.
black_comedy.how: two of its three sources read directly and the remaining one from a search summary, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: genre-wide: Credible reference works define black comedy as a kind of comedy (farce and low comedy per Britannica), so comic timing follows from the genre’s definition across all of it. The support is definitional only: no acting source states it, and the deadpan link remains unsupported, so confidence stays low.

black_comedy.uncertainty: Britannica couldn’t be opened, so it was read only as a search summary. No acting or training source ties a particular comic technique to black comedy: the idea of deadpan, of playing it straight, appears only in general comedy advice and in blogs that aren’t credible. It holds for the whole genre only by definition, and no source states a technical convention, so it stays at low confidence.

blaxploitation.claim: Scholarship characterizes the blaxploitation movement by, among other things, excessive violence, and describes its black action cinema as heroes, male and female, deploying violence, guns and martial arts. Stars doing their own stunts is attested only for individuals such as Pam Grier.
blaxploitation.source: Novotny Lawrence, Blaxploitation Films of the 1970s: Blackness and Genre (Routledge, 2008), https://www.routledge.com/Blaxploitation-Films-of-the-1970s-Blackness-and-Genre/Lawrence/p/book/9780415540957 [read directly]; Yvonne Tasker, Action and Adventure Films (Schirmer Encyclopedia of Film, via Encyclopedia.com, 2007), https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/action-and-adventure-films [read directly]; Museum of UnCut Funk, Karate, Kung Fu and Blaxploitation (Google Arts & Culture, n.d.), https://artsandculture.google.com/story/karate-kung-fu-and-blaxploitation-museum-of-uncut-funk/rQXRbvxKvFtImw?hl=en [read directly]
blaxploitation.sourceSupports: Blaxploitation Films of the 1970s: Blackness and Genre: Publisher description: the movement "is characterized by films that feature a black hero or heroine, black supporting characters, a predominately black urban setting, a display of black sexuality, excessive violence, and a contemporary rhythm and blues soundtrack." Also: "Blaxploitation films were made across varying genres" (detective, horror, gangster, cop action). Action and Adventure Films: "The 1970s also saw the emergence of black action cinema (sometimes called 'blaxploitation') with both male and female heroes deploying violence, gun power, and martial arts against oppressive enemies and institutions." Karate, Kung Fu and Blaxploitation: "The 1970's marked the beginning of the one-two combination of Blaxploitation and Kung Fu"; Jim Kelly’s "superb karate skills". It doesn’t say how common fights were across the cycle, or whether stars did their own.
blaxploitation.how: all three of its sources read directly, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: genre-wide: Two independent scholarly sources characterize the movement as a whole by violence (Lawrence: 'excessive violence' as a defining feature across the genres it spans; Tasker: heroes deploying violence, guns and martial arts). On-screen violence is staged combat, so fight and stunt work is a genre convention. Two sources and an inference from 'violence' to staged combat keep it at medium. Grier doing her own stunts is one star and isn’t the basis.

blaxploitation.uncertainty: Lawrence’s 'excessive violence' comes from the publisher’s description of his book, not a page of the book itself. Violence includes gunplay, which asks less of the actor than hand-to-hand fights. Horror entries such as Blacula fit the cycle but aren’t action films. 'Larger-than-life star presence' still has no source. Fights And Stunts is inferred from the cycle’s violence, and no source states fight work for the genre as a whole, so it stays at low confidence.

body_horror.claim: Body horror built on practical effects puts its actors in heavy prosthetics for long makeup sessions, at real physical cost. The Substance had five- to eight-hour applications.
body_horror.source: Backstage, 'How The Substance Created Its Body Horror With Practical Effects', https://www.backstage.com/magazine/article/the-substance-makeup-artist-effects-interview-78270/; CNN, 'Margaret Qualley says her skin took a year to recover from The Substance prosthetics', https://www.cnn.com/2025/01/16/style/margaret-qualley-the-substance-prosthetics-intl-scli
body_horror.sourceSupports: From a search summary: full-body makeup took seven hours, more complex applications five to five and a half; Demi Moore or Margaret Qualley spent six to eight hours in makeup on the heaviest days; the production chose practical effects 'like those out of The Fly'. CNN: Qualley’s skin took about a year to recover from the prosthetics.

tags.why: The sources describe prosthetic transformation as the actor’s working condition on a body-horror film.

body_horror.uncertainty: There’s one film, plus a reference to The Fly. Body horror done with digital effects wouldn’t ask this, so Physical Transformation rests on practical-effects practice. 'Conveying pain and loss of bodily control' isn’t supported by these sources. On review (October 10, 2026), one film’s practical-effects prosthetics weren’t enough to make it a requirement of the whole genre.

buddy_comedy.claim: The buddy comedy is a comedy subgenre built on two contrasting leads, and its formula gives the actors room to show chemistry and comic timing. Comedy teams such as Laurel and Hardy and Hope and Crosby are part of its lineage.
buddy_comedy.source: Backstage staff (byline not verified), The Best Buddy Cop Movies of All Time (Backstage, unknown), https://www.backstage.com/magazine/article/best-buddy-cop-movies-77133/ [from a search summary]; Backstage staff (byline not verified), Film Genres: An Introduction to Basic Movie Categories (Backstage, unknown), https://www.backstage.com/magazine/article/movie-genres-76034/ [from a search summary]; Wes D. Gehring, Comedy (Schirmer Encyclopedia of Film, via Encyclopedia.com, 2007), https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/comedy [read directly]
buddy_comedy.sourceSupports: The Best Buddy Cop Movies of All Time: The buddy comedy formula involves two opposites coming together to fight crime and often each other, 'providing the actors playing them plenty of room to demonstrate chemistry and comedic timing'. The page couldn’t be opened, so this is from a search summary. Film Genres: An Introduction to Basic Movie Categories: It lists the 'buddy' picture among the subgenres of comedy, alongside slapstick, satire, farce, parody. The page couldn’t be opened, so this is from a search summary. Comedy: It discusses comedy teams, such as Laurel and Hardy’s 'tit-for-tat exchanges of comic violence' and the 'inspired teaming' of Hope and Crosby in the Road pictures. It doesn’t state an acting demand for buddy films specifically.
buddy_comedy.how: one of its three sources read directly and the other two from search summaries, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: genre-wide: Buddy comedy is a comedy subgenre by definition, and a trade source for actors states directly that its formula asks the leads for comedic timing (and chemistry). Raised to medium only on that direct statement, with the caveat that it was read as a snippet.

buddy_comedy.uncertainty: Neither Backstage page could be opened, so the wording rests on search summaries, and the timing sentence comes from a list of buddy-cop films. Only one publisher states it. Chemistry isn’t one of the requirements the game can ask for. The buddy film outside comedy (buddy action, buddy drama) asks for no comedy. The one direct statement (Backstage) was read only as a search summary, so it stays at low confidence: a buddy comedy is a comedy, but that’s a definition, not evidence of a technical convention.

buddy_cop.claim: Academic studies describe the buddy-cop film as an action-comedy hybrid: known for action and best known for its comedy, with witty banter, snappy one-liners and over-the-top stunts as hallmarks.
buddy_cop.source: Briah Baker, Why Can't We Be Friends: The Legitimization of Police Violence in the Buddy-Cop Film Genre (University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee (MA thesis, Media Studies), 2021), https://minds.wisc.edu/bitstream/handle/1793/92734/Baker_uwm_0263M_13037.pdf [read directly]; Sidney Garner (mentor Dr. Charlene Regester), On and Off Screen: Race in Buddy Cop Films (UNC Chapel Hill, MURAP 2020 paper (Carolina Digital Repository), 2020), https://cdr.lib.unc.edu/downloads/gf06gb38m?locale=en [read directly]
buddy_cop.sourceSupports: Why Can’t We Be Friends: The Legitimization of Police Violence in the Buddy-Cop Film Genre: 'the witty banter, the over the top stunts, and the fast pace action that are hallmarks of the genre'; 'The action-comedy relies on the witty comebacks and snappy one-liners of the characters in the film to cut the tension in violent' scenes; Lethal Weapon 'features big explosions, car chases, extreme stunt-work'. On and Off Screen: Race in Buddy Cop Films: 'Known for its comradery, action, and comedy, this genre...'; 'The buddy cop genre, aside from action, is known best for its use of comedy.'
buddy_cop.how: both its sources read directly, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: genre-wide: Two independent academic works state comedy (banter, one-liners) as a defining convention of the genre as a whole, not of one film.

genre-wide: Both works name action as a genre convention; Baker names 'over the top stunts' and fast-paced action as hallmarks of the genre. The tag fits the leads' fight and action work; much stunt work is doubled in practice.

buddy_cop.uncertainty: Both sources are student works (an MA thesis and an undergraduate research paper), not peer-reviewed; Baker’s 'hallmarks' line is in her personal preface. Neither speaks about what actors train for. The Rush Hour split of stunts and comedy between partners remains one franchise, not a convention. Comedy-led entries such as Ride Along may lean less on combat. Student works don’t establish a convention, so it stays at low confidence.

caper.claim: No credible source on performing in caper films was found.
caper.source: None credible. The search on Ocean's Eleven returned fan wikis and Grokipedia, which weren’t used
caper.sourceSupports: The search found nothing usable. The low-quality pages repeated praise of Ocean’s Eleven’s 'ensemble cast chemistry' and 'witty dialogue'.
caper.uncertainty: The genre is defined as lighter in tone and witty, but no cited source states it, so the research didn’t name Comic Timing for it. Charm, light timing and ensemble play remain unsourced.

chanbara.claim: Chanbara is by name the sword-fighting film, and its actors perform tate: choreographed stage and screen sword-fighting built from memorized fixed forms.
chanbara.source: GATE 12, 'Tokyo Samurai Stage Fighting: Japanese Minds in the Art of Tate Sword-Fighting', https://thegate12.com/article/283; Wikipedia, 'Samurai cinema' (pointer only), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samurai_cinema
chanbara.sourceSupports: From a search summary: chanbara means 'sword fighting' films, from the onomatopoeia 'chan-chan-bara-bara', and is a sub-category of jidaigeki. Tate is 'stage fighting in brawls or with swords, in stage plays and movies' whose 'movements come in fixed forms, which are memorized and combined by many actors to create a flashy sword fight'. The Shinkokugeki troupe was known for realistic tate.

tags.why: The genre is defined by swordfights, and the tate source says actors memorize and perform the fight forms.

chanbara.uncertainty: The pages weren’t read directly, but the genre’s own name calls for it. Period movement, stillness and period speech aren’t supported by these sources, so the research didn’t name Heightened Language.

chase.claim: Reference works define the chase film as an early and silent-era form in which a chase is the primary element, built on editing and on crowds running from one place to the next; its comic branch, from music-hall chase skits to Sennett’s Keystone chases, is physical comedy. No credible source makes stunts or fight work a convention of the form.
chase.source: Charlie Keil, Early Cinema (Schirmer Encyclopedia of Film, via Encyclopedia.com, 2007), https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/early-cinema [read directly]; Annette Kuhn and Guy Westwell, Chase film (entry in A Dictionary of Film Studies) (Oxford University Press (Oxford Reference), 2020), https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/acref/9780198832096.001.0001/acref-9780198832096-e-0102 [from a search summary]; Tamar Jeffers McDonald, Slapstick Comedy (Schirmer Encyclopedia of Film, via Encyclopedia.com, 2007), https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/slapstick-comedy [read directly]
chase.sourceSupports: Early Cinema: In chase films "large groups of people run from one locale to the next, the cut introducing a new setting while sustaining the sense of frantic movement"; the effect rests on "the accelerated sensation of displacement and mobility editing helps to promote." Chase film (entry in A Dictionary of Film Studies): From a search summary, as the page couldn’t be opened: chase films are films of the early and silent eras in which a chase is the primary element, with precedent in music-hall and vaudeville comedy chase skits 'punctuated with pratfalls and physical comedy'. Slapstick Comedy: Sennett realized "the comic potential of the chase"; his films ended with Kops and others who "careen across the screen, fall over, collide, and generally create mayhem."
chase.how: two of its three sources read directly and the remaining one from a search summary, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: unsupported: The reference works define the chase film by editing and pursuit, not by what performers do. The only actor-level evidence found earlier (Tom Cruise running his own chases) is one star. The comic chase points to physical comedy, not fights and stunts, and that is a different tag that wasn’t proposed.

chase.uncertainty: The Oxford entry was seen only as a search summary. Modern car-chase action films are usually classed as action films, not as 'chase films', and their driving is mostly done by stunt drivers.

childrens.claim: No source on the acting style of children’s films was found. The sources found were about directing child actors.
childrens.source: Angela Dalle Vacche, 'Directing Children in Cinema and the Double Meaning of Self-Consciousness', https://homes.lmc.gatech.edu/~dallevacche/style/articles/DirectingChildren.pdf; Videomaker, 'Directing Children', https://www.videomaker.com/article/c14/13549-directing-children/
childrens.sourceSupports: From a search summary: De Sica directed children by miming what they were to do; children respond to spontaneity and scenes can be made into games. These describe child actors in any genre, not films made for children.
childrens.uncertainty: Neither 'warm, clear, energetic playing readable by young audiences' nor the share of child actors in children’s films is supported. The genre’s definition calls for none of the requirements the game can ask for.

christmas.claim: Backstage advice on Hallmark-style Christmas films is to play sincerity and earnestness, delivering even cheesy lines with conviction and pitching emotion big rather than subtle.
christmas.sourceSupports: From a search summary: 'The primary focus should be on sincerity and earnestness, especially when delivering lines about Christmas magic'; actors should 'play it big'; successful actors 'infuse even the cheesiest dialogue with earnest desire'.
christmas.uncertainty: This covers Hallmark’s Christmas TV movies only. The game defines a Christmas film as combinable with any genre, so what it asks would follow the genre it’s combined with. None of the requirements the game can ask for fits 'sincere warmth'.

coming_of_age.claim: Several noted coming-of-age films are praised for naturalistic performances, some from nonprofessional young actors with improvised dialogue, but no source treats this as a convention of the genre.
coming_of_age.source: StudioBinder, 'Naturalist Movies — Characteristics of Naturalism in Film', https://www.studiobinder.com/blog/naturalist-movies-examples/; Mental Floss, 'The 25 Best Coming-of-Age Films', https://www.mentalfloss.com/posts/best-coming-of-age-movies
coming_of_age.sourceSupports: From a search summary: The 400 Blows has a 'wonderfully naturalistic performance' from Jean-Pierre Léaud; The Florida Project cast nonprofessional children, and 'improvised actions and dialogue between the kids' are cited as naturalist traits; The Breakfast Club’s library confession scene was 'mostly improvised'.
coming_of_age.uncertainty: These are examples, not a convention. Improvisation and Naturalism On Camera were considered and left out, because the sources don’t tie them to the genre.

concert_film.claim: A concert film records an extended live performance by musicians (bands, singers) or sometimes stand-up comedians, before an audience. Its performers are playing themselves live, not acting roles, and singing is common but not universal.
concert_film.source: Ron Deutsch, Docs That Really Rock: Music Documentaries Go Beyond the Performance (International Documentary Association (documentary.org), 2014), https://www.documentary.org/feature/docs-really-rock-music-documentaries-go-beyond-performance [read directly]; Wikipedia contributors, Concert film (Wikipedia (pointer only), 2026), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concert_film [from a search summary]
concert_film.sourceSupports: Docs That Really Rock: Music Documentaries Go Beyond the Performance: The concert/performance film, with Woodstock (1970) as 'the basic template', may include interstitial sequences 'but it’s primarily about watching a performance'. Jonathan Demme: it documents 'a musical event that happened and was attended by ticket-buying people'. Concert film: Used only as a lead, it defines the subject as an extended live music performance; other glossaries add stand-up comedians.
concert_film.how: one of its two sources read directly and the other from a search summary, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: subgenre-or-role: Live musical performance is genre-wide, but singing isn’t: instrumental acts and comedians are covered. Singing belongs to concert films of vocal acts, and the performers are musicians performing as themselves, not actors executing a technique.

concert_film.uncertainty: No scholarly reference work defining the genre was read: the IDA article is a trade source. None of the requirements the game can ask for is playing an instrument or live music, so Singing is a stretch. Whether an acted character belongs in a concert film at all is a question for the game, not the research.
concert_film.belongsTo: concert films of singers and vocal acts, where the performers sing as themselves

conspiracy_thriller.claim: Only critics’ writing on one film was found: The Conversation, the high point of the 1970s paranoia thriller, is praised for Hackman’s subdued, interior performance of rising paranoia.
conspiracy_thriller.source: Emanuel Levy, 'Conversation, The (1974)', https://emanuellevy.com/review/conversation-the-7/; The Film Experience, 'Almost There: Gene Hackman in The Conversation', http://thefilmexperience.net/blog/2024/4/8/almost-there-gene-hackman-in-the-conversation.html
conspiracy_thriller.sourceSupports: From a search summary: the film is 'a subdued, existential exploration' and 'the peak of the paranoia thriller craze'; Hackman plays 'someone who’s turned himself into a non-person' and conveys panic when he learns he is being tapped.
conspiracy_thriller.uncertainty: These are one film’s reviews. Restrained paranoia isn’t documented as something the genre asks. None of the requirements the game can ask for fits it.

cosmic_horror.claim: Lovecraftian stories typically end with the protagonist’s sanity cracking, and Backstage advises actors to track that descent and often play it as quiet detachment rather than ranting.
cosmic_horror.source: Backstage, 'Cosmic Horror Movies for Filmmakers + Actors to Watch', https://www.backstage.com/magazine/article/cosmic-horror-movies-77754/; Wikipedia, 'Lovecraftian horror' (pointer only), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lovecraftian_horror
cosmic_horror.sourceSupports: From a search summary, Backstage: 'madness takes many forms and isn’t always ranting and raving ... it’s important to carefully track the role’s emotional journey and find ways to subtly portray a detachment from reality.' Wikipedia: a staple ending is that the protagonist 'perceives the unexplainable horror and the enormity of it cracks their sanity'. The Backstage page couldn’t be opened.
cosmic_horror.uncertainty: None of the requirements the game can ask for fits a portrayal of a mind unraveling. Reacting to what can’t be shown isn’t supported by these sources: see the Creature Feature genre for the evidence on reacting to nothing.

costume_drama.claim: Period drama asks actors to learn period movement and behavior (deportment, greetings, bows, sitting and walking in period clothes, period dances) and sometimes period speech, and conservatories teach it as its own discipline.
costume_drama.source: RADA, 'Period Movement for Actors', https://www.rada.ac.uk/short-courses/period-movement-actors/; HB Studio, 'Period Style', https://www.hbstudio.org/classes/physical-acting-techniques/period-style/; Backstage, 'What is a Period Piece?', https://www.backstage.com/magazine/article/how-to-approach-acting-in-a-period-piece-72139/
costume_drama.sourceSupports: RADA (read directly): the course examines 'deportment, greetings, social interaction, clothing, and dance' and 'period-specific movement, style and codes of behaviour' from the Elizabethan and Jacobean courts to the 1920s. A search summary of the other results: 'A corset ... changes how you breathe, how you sit, how you bend'; actors consult 'a speech and voice teacher, as well as a movement teacher, to find the most specific tempos, rhythms, pronunciations, and specific physical movements that are truest to the period'. Which page carries the speech-teacher sentence wasn’t checked.
costume_drama.uncertainty: RADA’s course is evidence that period movement is a taught skill. It doesn’t say every costume drama demands it. Period dance appears in RADA’s syllabus, but the research didn’t name Dancing, because no source says costume dramas require it. Heightened Language, which is about language, fit this movement only loosely, and the review of October 10, 2026 took it away: it’s verse and rhetoric, and the research is about period movement and deportment, which none of the requirements the game can ask for covers.

courtroom_drama.claim: Only weak sources were found: actor-training blogs note that a lawyer’s closing argument should be played as rehearsed, polished and fully memorized.
courtroom_drama.source: TBell Actors Studio, 'How to Prepare a Monologue', https://tbellactorsstudio.com/blog/how-to-prepare-a-monologue/; Persuadius, '16 Trial Presentation Tips You Can Learn from Hollywood', https://persuadius.com/blog/bid/59680/16-trial-presentation-tips-you-can-learn-from-hollywood
courtroom_drama.sourceSupports: From a search summary: an actor playing a lawyer giving a closing argument is 'very prepared, polished and very memorized compared to other characters'; long monologues should be broken into beats. Which page holds the first sentence wasn’t checked.
courtroom_drama.uncertainty: No credible source ties long speeches or restraint under cross-examination to the genre as an acting demand. None of the requirements the game can ask for fits.

creature_feature.claim: Creature films with practical creatures have used a recognized specialty, the creature or prosthetic performer, who acts head to toe in suits and prosthetics with restricted sight and hearing. That demand belongs to the creature role, not to the human cast.
creature_feature.source: James Ostime, Doug Jones, Unmasked (Interview Magazine, 2013), https://www.interviewmagazine.com/culture/doug-jones-falling-skies [read directly]; Witney Seibold, The Shape Of Water And Pan's Labyrinth Were Very Different Prosthetics Experiences For Doug Jones (SlashFilm, 2022), https://www.slashfilm.com/1021091/the-shape-of-water-and-pans-labyrinth-were-very-different-prosthetics-experiences-for-doug-jones/ [read directly]; NPR, Creature Actor Doug Jones Shares How He Transforms Into Movie Monsters (NPR, 2018), https://www.npr.org/2018/02/22/588069904/creature-actor-doug-jones-shares-how-he-transforms-into-movie-monsters [from a search summary]
creature_feature.sourceSupports: Doug Jones, Unmasked: Jones: 'I’m one of the top "makeup actors" in the movie business, appearing head to toe in prosthetic pieces and elaborate costumes.' The Shape Of Water And Pan’s Labyrinth Were Very Different Prosthetics Experiences For Doug Jones: Jones: 'Any creature suit that I’ve worn over the last 31 years hampers your eyesight, your hearing'; Pan’s Labyrinth makeup took five to six hours, The Shape of Water three. Creature Actor Doug Jones Shares How He Transforms Into Movie Monsters: Only its title was read, as the page didn’t load. It names 'creature actor' as a role, and transformation into monsters.
creature_feature.how: two of its three sources read directly and the remaining one from a search summary, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: subgenre-or-role: The sources document transformation as the job of the creature performer, a specialist role, and only where the creature is practical (suit or prosthetic). Human leads aren’t asked for it, and CGI creatures remove the role.

creature_feature.uncertainty: The sources center on one performer (Doug Jones) whose films (Pan’s Labyrinth, The Shape of Water) are fantasy as much as creature features. No source states the suit performer as a convention of the creature feature as a whole. The claim about reacting to nothing was general visual-effects practice, and isn’t used here.
creature_feature.belongsTo: the creature performer role in practical-effects (suit or prosthetic) creature films

crime.claim: No credible source on what the crime genre asks of actors was found.
crime.source: None credible. Wikipedia, 'Gangster film' (pointer only), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gangster_film, gives the AFI definition; the other results were IMDb lists and Screen Rant rankings
crime.sourceSupports: Wikipedia quotes the American Film Institute defining the gangster film as 'centered on organized crime or maverick criminals in a twentieth century setting'. That is about subject, not performance.
crime.uncertainty: The genre is too broad to carry a single performance demand. Grounded, morally ambiguous characterization and menace remain unsourced. The genre’s definition calls for none of the requirements the game can ask for.

cyberpunk.claim: Cyberpunk is defined by setting and theme (dystopian high-tech cities, corporate power, outsider protagonists, noir influence), not by fight work. The Matrix’s cast trained for months with Yuen Woo-ping because the directors expected them to do many of their own stunts; that is one film.
cyberpunk.source: Mark Salisbury, The Matrix: how the Wachowskis changed sci-fi (BFI, 2019), https://www.bfi.org.uk/features/matrix-wachowskis-keanu-reeves [read directly]; Rafael Abreu, What is Cyberpunk? Genre Definition, Origins & Examples (StudioBinder, 2025), https://www.studiobinder.com/blog/what-is-cyberpunk-definition/ [read directly]
cyberpunk.sourceSupports: The Matrix: how the Wachowskis changed sci-fi: "The Wachowskis expected their cast to do many of their own stunts, and so Reeves and co spent months training with legendary Hong Kong martial arts choreographer and director Yuen Woo-ping." Its account of the film’s influence is about cinematography, costume and comic-book films, not about cyberpunk acting. What is Cyberpunk? Genre Definition, Origins & Examples: It defines cyberpunk as "a science-fiction sub-genre dealing with the integration of society and technology in dystopian settings" and lists setting, technology, outsider protagonists, noir influence and transhumanist themes. It mentions no fights, martial arts or acting demands. It’s an industry education site, used only for the definition.
cyberpunk.how: both its sources read directly, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: subgenre-or-role: The documented fight and wire training belongs to The Matrix and the action strand it inspired, not to cyberpunk as defined. Definitions of the genre name no fight work, and core titles such as Blade Runner aren’t fight-driven.

cyberpunk.uncertainty: No credible source was found that says post-Matrix cyberpunk films as a group adopted wire-fu; the claims seen to that effect were on fan or listicle sites. The SCMP page from the earlier research couldn’t be opened, and wasn’t read again.
cyberpunk.belongsTo: action-led cyberpunk in the mold of The Matrix, with its martial-arts and wirework set pieces

dance.claim: Screendance asks its performers for trained dance: choreographed movement made specifically to be filmed, shaped with the camera and the edit.
dance.source: San Francisco Conservatory of Dance, Dance Theory Glossary: 'Screendance' — https://sfconservatoryofdance.org/dance-theory-glossary/screendance/; corroborated by BFI, 'Maya Deren: 7 films that guarantee her legend' — https://www.bfi.org.uk/features/maya-deren-meshes-of-the-afternoon
dance.sourceSupports: SFCD: 'Screendance, also known as dance film or dance on screen, is a genre of filmmaking that combines dance and cinematography'; the dancers’ movement is 'captured and presented on screen' with multiple angles, close-ups and editing that 'highlight the nuances of the choreography and the dancers' performances.' BFI: in A Study in Choreography for Camera, 'Dancer Talley Beatty moves freely ... with careful choreographed movements'; Deren 'collaborated with ... Antony Tudor, who brought a young crew of ballet dancers.'

tags.why: The conservatory glossary defines the genre as combining dance and cinematography, with the dancers’ performances as its subject; BFI names trained dancers (Talley Beatty, Tudor’s ballet dancers) as its performers.

dance.uncertainty: Neither source speaks to stamina or to repeating choreography across takes; that part of the earlier reading is unsourced. A search summary (edukatesg.com, not used) says dancers need screen-specific timing before the shoot day.

dark_fantasy.claim: Dark-fantasy creature roles can ask an actor for hours of prosthetic makeup and a physically draining performance through it, sometimes in a language the actor doesn’t speak.
dark_fantasy.sourceSupports: Jones: the Faun and Pale Man makeups 'were both about five hours'; 'I couldn’t sit in a conventional chair... with the ram horns on the head, to hold my head up was like ugh, I can’t take it anymore.' He learned his Spanish lines phonetically. Wikipedia’s 'Dark fantasy' and 'Creature actor' pages (used only as leads) define the genre as fantasy with horror’s grim elements and a creature actor as one who plays a being of radically different appearance using suits or prosthetics.

tags.why: Jones describes five-hour prosthetic makeups and a leg contraption for creature roles in Pan’s Labyrinth, a canonical dark fantasy.

dark_fantasy.uncertainty: This is one actor in one film, and a creature-performer specialism; the source doesn’t say that every lead in dark fantasy does prosthetic work. 'Morally ambiguous characterisation' from the earlier reading is unsourced. On review (October 10, 2026), one actor in one creature role wasn’t enough to make it a requirement of the whole genre.

detective.claim: Long-running detective roles have asked actors for exhaustive character research, and in some versions for an accent and for rapid, exact delivery of deduction speeches.
detective.source: Strand Magazine, 'Interview: David Suchet' — https://strandmag.com/the-magazine/interviews/david-suchet/; search summaries on Benedict Cumberbatch's Sherlock (Collider interview, https://collider.com/benedict-cumberbatch-interview-sherlock-war-horse-spielberg/, not read directly)
detective.sourceSupports: Suchet: he 'plowed through most of Agatha Christie’s novels' compiling a file of Poirot’s characteristics; 'I was desperate that he should sound French'; Poirot’s mannerisms 'have to be real and not jokey.' Search summaries, secondhand, say Cumberbatch found the deduction scenes hard because they 'have to be spot on' and involved a large volume of lines.
detective.uncertainty: Both sources are about single famous characters, not the genre. Poirot’s accent belongs to the character, not to detective fiction, so the research didn’t name Accents. No source was found that says detective drama as a form asks a particular skill; the claim about expository revelation scenes rests on a search summary about one series.

disaster.claim: Disaster films can put actors through weeks of physically punishing practical work, such as water-tank sequences done in person rather than by doubles.
disaster.source: Prokerala, ''The Impossible' was physically and emotionally demanding: Naomi Watts' — https://www.prokerala.com/people/interviews/the-impossible-was-physically-and-emotionally-demanding-naomi-watts-interview.html
disaster.sourceSupports: Watts: 'I had to stay in a water tank for weeks. (So) it was quite physically demanding for me'; 'we were anchored into a chair with weights on us ... the chair starts spinning, and you have to do all your arm-acting and head-flipping'; underwater work meant holding her breath. Search summaries of NPR (not read directly) and Wikipedia add 'probably the most physically demanding thing I’ve ever done' and five weeks in the tank with Tom Holland.

tags.why: Watts describes performing weighted, spinning underwater sequences herself across weeks in a tank: sustained physical action by the actor.

disaster.uncertainty: It’s one film. A search summary of a blog, secondhand, reports Ernest Borgnine calling The Poseidon Adventure his most physically demanding film; that isn’t verified. No source was found on large-ensemble panic work as a convention. On review (October 10, 2026), one film’s water-tank work wasn’t enough to make it a requirement of the whole genre.
disaster.belongsTo: productions that shoot their peril practically

docudrama.claim: Docudrama asks actors to stand in for real, often recent or living, people, and the audience judges the performance against what it already knows of them.
docudrama.source: Jonathan Bignell, 'Docudrama performance: realism, recognition and representation', in Christine Cornea (ed.), Genre and Performance: Film and Television (Manchester University Press, 2010), pp. 59-75 — https://centaur.reading.ac.uk/17671/1/Docudrama_Performance.pdf; Britannica Dictionary, 'docudrama' — https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/docudrama
docudrama.sourceSupports: Bignell (only the abstract, through a search, as the PDF couldn’t be opened): docudrama’s performers invite viewers to judge them in relation to real events and other media representations, evaluating 'the performance of the real' against prior knowledge. Britannica Dictionary: 'a movie that is usually made for television and that tells a story about real events that have happened recently.' A search summary of Backstage ('The Actor as Interviewer', not read directly) says actors in a docudrama about the People’s Temple interviewed survivors and noted clothing, voice and mannerisms.

tags.why: Bignell’s abstract places recognition of the real person at the center of docudrama performance; the Backstage summary has actors noting the voice and mannerisms of the people they’ll play. This is character work led by impersonation, not prosthetics.

docudrama.uncertainty: The scholarly chapter was read only as an abstract. Whether Physical Transformation, which the game trains as Character Work, is the right skill for impersonation is a judgment call; no source mentions prosthetics or makeup for docudrama.

documentary.claim: Actors in documentaries mostly appear as voices reading letters or narration, or as performers in reenactments, sometimes lip-syncing to real interview audio.
documentary.source: Bonnie Yates, 'On the Use of Actors and Re-enactments in Documentaries', Alternative Considerations of Jonestown and Peoples Temple (San Diego State University) — https://jonestown.sdsu.edu/?page_id=81711; Girish Shambu, 'Past Performance: Reviving Reenactment', Film Comment — https://www.filmcomment.com/blog/past-performance-reviving-reenactment-girish-shambu-documentary/
documentary.sourceSupports: Yates: reenactments 'provide a context, to show what things looked or sounded like'; on voice-overs, 'the tone of voice used by the actor is likely to give the audience the impression that the individual quoted was, indeed, given to the emotion associated with that tone.' Shambu: in The Arbor 'actors lip-sync to audio recordings of Dunbar’s family members, following the practices of "verbatim theater"'; in Framing Agnes the performers’ lines 'are drawn from the original interview transcripts.'

tags.why: Yates describes actors voicing the quoted words of real people in documentary voice-overs, and that their tone shapes the meaning.

documentary.uncertainty: Neither source says how common actor narration is relative to narration by the filmmaker or a presenter. 'Little conventional acting' is a reasonable reading of the form but no source states it.

domestic_drama.claim: Domestic drama descends from the realist and naturalist stage, which asked for psychologically real acting and for ensemble playing in place of the star turn.
domestic_drama.source: From search summaries: Britannica, 'Stanislavsky system' — https://www.britannica.com/art/Stanislavsky-system (couldn’t be opened); fiveable, 'Realist and Naturalist theater' — https://fiveable.me/18th-and-19th-century-literature/unit-6/realist-naturalist-theater/study-guide/IoXCgOsbj4UmitM2
domestic_drama.sourceSupports: Britannica (from a search summary): Stanislavsky 'began with attempts to find a style of acting more appropriate to the greater realism of 20th-century drama than the histrionic acting styles of the 19th century.' Fiveable (a study guide, from a search summary): the Meiningen Players 'pioneered the concept of ensemble acting'; realist theater 'emphasized ensemble acting, with all members of the cast working together to create a cohesive, believable world.'
domestic_drama.uncertainty: The sources concern realist and naturalist drama (Ibsen, Chekhov, Strindberg), the tradition domestic drama belongs to, not 'domestic drama' by name. They describe stage acting, so they don’t support Naturalism On Camera. Britannica couldn’t be opened, so it wasn’t read directly.

drama.claim: Serious drama in the modern tradition asks for realistic, emotionally truthful acting, the aim of Stanislavsky’s system and the training built on it.
drama.sourceSupports: From search summaries, as the pages couldn’t be opened: the system was an attempt to find acting 'more appropriate to the greater realism of 20th-century drama'; it 'emphasizes actors drawing on emotional memory and intense inner identification with their characters.'
drama.uncertainty: Britannica couldn’t be opened, so the wording is from search summaries. 'Drama' is too broad for any one of the requirements the game can ask for, and emotional truth isn’t one of them. No source ties Naturalism On Camera to drama as such.

dystopian.claim: No source was found for what dystopian fiction as a genre asks of actors. One production, Children of Men, asked for rehearsed choreography of long takes.
dystopian.source: Search summaries about Children of Men (Wikipedia, used only as a lead — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men; Wellesnet — https://wellesnet.com/alfonso-curarons-children-of-men-a-tribute-to-orson-welles-and-the-long-take/)
dystopian.sourceSupports: From search summaries: Cuarón shot as many long takes as possible; 'the long takes required a higher level of choreography from cast and crew' and more rehearsal time. Search summaries of Collider praise restrained performances in The Hunger Games films, which is a critic’s opinion, not a statement of what the genre asks.
dystopian.uncertainty: No source found supports 'suppressed fear and restrained, controlled performance' as a genre demand. The long-take choreography belongs to one director’s method, not to dystopian fiction.

eco_horror.claim: No source was found for what eco-horror asks of actors. One production report says the Annihilation cast weren’t told when a creature would attack, to get real reactions.
eco_horror.source: Search summaries (Collider, 'Natalie Portman on What Alex Garland Did That Surprised Cast' — https://collider.com/natalie-portman-annihilation-interview/, not read directly)
eco_horror.sourceSupports: From a search summary: 'the cast wasn’t aware when a monster would come out and attack them during a particular sequence, adding to the authentic reactions captured on screen.'
eco_horror.uncertainty: It’s one film, unverified. Calling Annihilation eco-horror is the search result’s placement, not a scholar’s. 'Survival-driven physical performance' and reacting to effects-generated threats as a genre demand are unsourced.

epic.claim: The epic is defined by scale, spectacle and large casts, not by an acting style. Physical prowess is tied to the hero in some strands (the Fairbanks swashbucklers, the sword-and-sandal peplum), and battle-heavy productions train their leads in combat, but no credible source makes combat a convention of the whole genre.
epic.source: Steve Neale, Epic Films (Schirmer Encyclopedia of Film, via Encyclopedia.com, 2007), https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/epic-films [read directly]; David Chapman (attribution from search listing, not verified), Breaking the Physique Barrier: Steve Reeves and the Promotion of Hercules (ResearchGate / LA84 digital library, unknown), https://www.researchgate.net/publication/277775916_Breaking_the_Physique_Barrier_Steve_Reeves_and_the_Promotion_of_Hercules [from a search summary]; Variety (byline not verified), Russell Crowe interview, Gladiator 20th anniversary (Variety, 2020), https://variety.com/2020/film/news/russell-crowe-interview-gladiator-20th-anniversary-1234596980/ [from a search summary]
epic.sourceSupports: Epic Films: It focuses on scale, spectacle, history and technology. On performers only: in Fairbanks’s 1920s epics 'the power of the central character to effect change is, however fancifully, bound up with his physical prowess'. It says nothing on battles, stunts or training as a requirement of the genre. Breaking the Physique Barrier: Steve Reeves and the Promotion of Hercules: After Hercules (1958), sword-and-sandal epics starred 'weight-trained actors'. This supports physique for the peplum subgenre, not combat for epics generally. The page couldn’t be opened. Russell Crowe interview, Gladiator 20th anniversary: Not read, as it’s behind a paywall. Earlier search summaries say Crowe trained for fighting and was injured; that’s one film only.
epic.how: one of its three sources read directly and the other two from search summaries, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: subgenre-or-role: The genre reference work names no combat or stunt convention. Combat training appears for battle-centered historical and sword-and-sandal epics and their warrior leads, documented film by film (Gladiator, Fairbanks), which isn’t a genre convention.

epic.uncertainty: The evidence for combat is anecdotal, production by production; the Variety interview and the peplum paper weren’t read. Many epics (biblical, biographical, romantic epics) have no combat lead.
epic.belongsTo: battle and sword-and-sandal epics, and their warrior and swashbuckler leads

erotic_thriller.claim: Erotic thrillers put choreographed intimate scenes at the center of the form, and productions now stage them with intimacy coordinators.
erotic_thriller.source: IndieWire, 'What Intimacy Coordinators Actually Do in Film and TV' — https://www.indiewire.com/features/craft/intimacy-coordinators-film-tv-role-explained-1235187325/ (behind a paywall; from a search summary)
erotic_thriller.sourceSupports: From search summaries: 'The sex scenes in the 1996 erotic crime thriller Bound were choreographed by ... Susie Bright, two decades before the "intimacy coordinator" title existed'; 'When doing a film like an erotic thriller or a psychosexual thriller, coordinators need to ensure the well being of the talent.'

tags.why: The source names the erotic thriller as a form whose sex scenes are choreographed by an intimacy specialist; the genre’s own definition (illicit romance or sexual fantasy) calls for such scenes.

erotic_thriller.uncertainty: The article couldn’t be read past the paywall. No source was found on the 'guarded, deceptive' playing the earlier reading claimed.

espionage.claim: The realist strand of the spy film has asked for extreme restraint and stillness, characters who keep everything in; the genre also runs to fantasy (Bond), so no single demand holds across it.
espionage.source: Slant Magazine, 'Interview: Tomas Alfredson, Gary Oldman, Colin Firth, and Peter Straughan on Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy' — https://www.slantmagazine.com/film/interview-cast-and-crew-of-tinker-tailor-soldier-spy/ (couldn’t be opened; from a search summary)
espionage.sourceSupports: From search summaries: Oldman, 'It’s interesting to be the motor of a scene, but from a very restrained, almost passive place'; he moved from 'dangerously emotional people' to 'people who have to keep everything so restrained and unemotional.' An NPR piece on The Spy (from a search summary) says Sacha Baron Cohen saw the real agent as sustaining a false identity like an actor.
espionage.uncertainty: This is one film’s approach. Naturalism On Camera was considered and left out: the restraint is described for le Carré adaptations only, and the genre’s own definition covers fantasy spy films too. Accents, disguise and action work are unsourced as things the genre asks.

experimental.claim: One canonical strand of experimental film, Maya Deren’s 'choreocinema', fused dance and film with trained dancers. Reference sources describe experimental film overall as non-narrative and convention-resisting, with no performance norm.
experimental.source: Georgia Korossi, Maya Deren: 7 films that guarantee her legend (BFI, 2017), https://www.bfi.org.uk/features/maya-deren-meshes-of-the-afternoon [read directly]; Bill Kte'pi, Experimental and Avant-Garde Film (EBSCO Research Starters, 2021), https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/film/experimental-and-avant-garde-film/ [read directly]
experimental.sourceSupports: Maya Deren: 7 films that guarantee her legend: Dance critic John Martin coined 'choreocinema' for 'the way Deren linked dance and film'; Deren worked with dancers Talley Beatty and Chao-Li Chi. It presents this as Deren’s distinctive contribution, not a general feature of experimental film. Experimental and Avant-Garde Film: Experimental film is 'principally non-narrative' and better understood as 'a type of method' than a genre; its only performance example is Warhol’s Sleep (poet John Giorno asleep), not dance.
experimental.how: both its sources read directly, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: subgenre-or-role: Dance belongs to the dance-film / choreocinema strand (Deren and successors), not to experimental film as a whole, which the reference source says has no defining performance convention.

experimental.uncertainty: Experimental film is defined by refusing conventions. Its documented performers include sleepers and non-actors as readily as dancers.
experimental.belongsTo: the dance-film strand of experimental film (choreocinema, or screendance)

exploitation.claim: Exploitation films were shot in days on tiny budgets with unknown actors, and their selling point was nudity, sex and gore, which the performers supplied.
exploitation.source: Eric Schaefer, 'Exploitation Films', Schirmer Encyclopedia of Film, via Encyclopedia.com — https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/exploitation-films
exploitation.sourceSupports: 'Their low budgets and accelerated shooting schedules meant that exploitation films featured stilted performances'; 'Shooting schedules were less than a week, with some films being shot in as little as two or three days'; scenes of spectacle included 'scenes in a nudist camp' and 'women performing striptease dances'; 'nudie-cuties'; sexploitation films; Blood Feast’s disemboweling.

tags.why: Schaefer describes nudity, striptease and sexploitation as the form’s core spectacle, performed by its cast.

exploitation.uncertainty: The source doesn’t say exploitation performers did their own stunts, so the research didn’t name Fights And Stunts. 'Broad, uninhibited performance' is unsourced; Schaefer calls the performances 'stilted', which is a result of the conditions, not something the genre asks.

fairy_tale.claim: No source was found for what fairy-tale film asks of actors.
fairy_tale.source: None found. Searches returned pantomime sources (such as Britannica, 'Mime and pantomime' — https://www.britannica.com/art/mime-and-pantomime), a distinct stage form
fairy_tale.sourceSupports: Pantomime sources, from search summaries, describe fairy tales as its source material and physical comedy and stock characters as its style; this is about British pantomime, not fairy-tale film.
fairy_tale.uncertainty: Archetypal, heightened characterization and prosthetics are unsourced. What pantomime asks wasn’t carried over to fairy tale, because that would stretch a source about another form.

family.claim: No source was found for what family film asks of actors. General references say the adult cast is often well-known stars, to widen the audience.
family.source: Wikipedia, 'Children's film' (pointer only) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children's_film; practitioner tips on child actors and animals, such as No Film School — https://nofilmschool.com/2017/02/4-tips-working-kids-and-animals-film-set (from a search summary)
family.sourceSupports: Wikipedia (from a search summary): 'In American family films, the adult cast can be composed of well known actors or actresses in an effort to attract a wider audience.' No Film School (from a search summary): kids and animals mean shoots take longer and sets run differently.
family.uncertainty: The child-and-animal sources address filmmakers, not genre demands on actors. 'Warm, accessible performance pitched to children and adults' is unsourced.

fantasy.claim: Major fantasy productions have taught their casts invented languages and purpose-built accents, and asked some actors for heavy physical transformation such as stilts and motion capture.
fantasy.source: Elvish Linguistic Fellowship, 'Languages in The Lord of the Rings movie' — https://www.elvish.org/gwaith/movie_news.htm; Daily Actor, 'Willem Dafoe on Becoming a Nine-Foot-Tall, Four-Armed Martian for John Carter' — https://www.dailyactor.com/film/willem-dafoe-john-carter/
fantasy.sourceSupports: Elvish.org: Andrew Jack and Roisín Carty were credited as 'Dialect and Creative Language Coaches' and Jack wrote an 'Accent Rationale' for the groups in the films and documented 'How Elijah Wood Learned Elvish.' Dafoe: 'I’m walking around on stilts on location'; 'we had to develop a vocabulary of gesture and the Martian spoken language'; the role meant 'not only would I perform on three-foot stilts'.

tags.why: The Lord of the Rings had dialect coaches who devised and taught accents for each group, plus Elvish.
Dafoe performed a nine-foot alien on stilts with motion capture and an invented gesture vocabulary.

fantasy.uncertainty: These are two productions, not the genre as a whole. John Carter is science fantasy. Green-screen acting is supported only by a search summary (Luke Evans, Den of Geek), and none of the requirements the game can ask for covers it. Combat training is unsourced. On review (October 10, 2026), two productions’ invented languages and transformations weren’t enough to make them requirements of the whole genre.
fantasy.belongsTo: particular productions with invented languages, and creature or motion-capture roles

film_noir.claim: Film noir’s performers carried the hard-boiled school’s terse, cynical dialogue, and the genre leaned on first-person voice-over narration spoken by its protagonists.
film_noir.source: Paul Schrader, 'Notes on Film Noir' (Film Comment, 1972), via search summaries of reproductions (such as https://fridaynightboys300.blogspot.com/2012/01/paul-schrader-notes-on-film-noir-part-1.html)
film_noir.sourceSupports: From search summaries: the hard-boiled writers 'created the "tough", cynical way of acting and thinking'; 'a love of romantic narration' in The Postman Always Rings Twice, Laura, Double Indemnity, The Lady from Shanghai, Out of the Past and Sunset Boulevard, where narration creates 'a mood of temps perdu'. A search summary of No Film School adds 'terse, understated vernacular peppered with laconic wisecracks'.

tags.why: Schrader lists voice-over narration as characteristic across canonical noirs; the narration is the actor’s voice-only performance.

film_noir.uncertainty: Schrader’s essay was seen only through reproductions and search summaries, not the original. Britannica’s film-noir entry couldn’t be opened. 'Cool, clipped delivery' as a performance demand is inferred from the dialogue style, not stated about actors.

folk_horror.claim: Folk horror is defined by landscape, isolation, a community’s skewed beliefs and a climactic ritual. In The Wicker Man the islanders perform folk songs and dance on screen, but that is one film, its lead’s singing wasn’t her own, and a scholar of the film calls horror films whose characters perform their own music exceptionally uncommon.
folk_horror.source: Dawn Keetley, Introduction: Defining Folk Horror (Revenant: Critical and Creative Studies of the Supernatural, issue 5 (Folk Horror), 2020), https://www.revenantjournal.com/contents/introduction-defining-folk-horror-2/ [read directly]; Jesse Pasternack, The Diegetic Folk Horrors of The Wicker Man (1973) (Establishing Shot (Indiana University blogs), 2023), https://blogs.iu.edu/establishingshot/2023/09/25/the-diegetic-folk-horrors-of-the-wicker-man-1973/ [read directly]; Don Kaye, The Wicker Man: Britt Ekland Goes Behind the Making of a Folk Horror Classic (Den of Geek, 2023), https://www.denofgeek.com/movies/the-wicker-man-britt-ekland-building-pagan-icon-horror/ [read directly]
folk_horror.sourceSupports: Introduction: Defining Folk Horror: Folk horror rests on invented folklore, deep landscape and a 'monstrous tribe' bound by belief; "The rituals that often conclude folk horror narratives ... bond the communities"; and it stresses "embodied traditions and rituals". It doesn’t name song or dance as conventions. The Diegetic Folk Horrors of The Wicker Man (1973): It describes bar patrons playing and singing 'The Landlord’s Daughter' and Willow joining a dance, and notes that horror films whose characters perform their own music are exceptionally uncommon. The Wicker Man: Britt Ekland Goes Behind the Making of a Folk Horror Classic: Ekland’s dialogue was dubbed by Annie Ross, and a body double was used for parts of the nude dance. (Search summaries add that Rachel Verney sang 'Willow’s Song'; that wasn’t read at the source.)
folk_horror.how: all three of its sources read directly, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: subgenre-or-role: On-screen folk song belongs to The Wicker Man and material that stages its rituals as song, not to the genre: Keetley’s definition names ritual but not song, and Pasternack calls character-performed music rare in horror. Even in The Wicker Man the lead’s singing was dubbed.

folk_horror.uncertainty: Scovell’s 'folk horror chain' (Folk Horror: Hours Dreadful and Things Strange, Auteur, 2017) was seen only through secondary summaries and names no song or dance. Recent films such as Midsommar stage ritual dance, but no credible source was found that generalizes it.
folk_horror.belongsTo: folk horror that stages its community ritual as performed folk song (The Wicker Man and films modeled on it)

gangster.claim: The gangster film’s stars defined a tough, physically marked performance style, and sound made hard-boiled dialogue and gunfire central to the form.
gangster.source: Dartmouth College Library, 'Film Genres: Gangster films' — https://researchguides.dartmouth.edu/filmgenres/gangsters; Kenneth Tynan, 'Cagney and the Mob', BFI Sight and Sound — https://www.bfi.org.uk/sight-and-sound/features/cagney-mob-kenneth-tynan-hollywoods-original-gangster
gangster.sourceSupports: Dartmouth: 'The gangster’s tough, masculine physical demeanour was marked in the performance styles of key stars such as James Cagney, Edward G. Robinson, Humphrey Bogart, and Paul Muni'; synchronized sound made 'hardboiled dialogue, gunfire, and screeching car tires' central. Tynan on Cagney: 'The spring-heeled walk, poised forward on the toes'; 'the rich, high-pitched, hectoring voice'; 'a beguiling capacity for reassuring while he murdered'.
gangster.uncertainty: None of the requirements the game can ask for fits a 'tough physical demeanour'. The regional and ethnic speech in the earlier reading is supported only by Wikipedia on The Godfather’s dialogue coach Al Lettieri, so the research didn’t name Accents. The violence is the characters’, and no source says actors do stunt work.

giallo.claim: Gialli were shot without sync sound, often with an international cast each speaking their own language in the same take, and the whole soundtrack, dialogue included, was dubbed afterwards.
giallo.source: CineMedia, 'In What Tongue Do Gialli Speak? Dubbing, Language, and the Affective Experience in Giallo Cinema' (no author shown) — https://cinemedia.media/in-what-tongue-do-gialli-speak/
giallo.sourceSupports: 'Italian films were almost exclusively shot without sync sound. Boom microphones were rarely used on set'; 'a British actor speaking English, an Italian actress speaking Italian, and a Spanish actor speaking Spanish—all in the very same take'; 'Voice actors were brought into recording booths to dub the dialogue into various languages.' A search summary of Backstage (not read directly) adds that English dubs often used the lead English-speaking actors’ own voices.

tags.why: The source makes post-synchronised voice performance in recording booths a standard part of how gialli were made. Caveat: much of it was done by dubbing actors rather than the on-screen cast.

giallo.uncertainty: Voice-Led Performance is weak for the on-screen actor: it’s strongest for English-speaking leads who re-voiced themselves, a claim resting on a search summary of Backstage. 'Stylised, heightened terror' is unsourced. The CineMedia piece names no author. On review (October 10, 2026), that wasn’t enough to make it a requirement of the whole genre.
giallo.belongsTo: English-speaking leads who re-voiced themselves in post-synchronization

gothic_horror.claim: No credible source found describes a heightened or declamatory acting convention for gothic horror film. Ranger’s study of the Georgian Gothic stage records vocal and physical casting requirements (a bass voice for older tragic roles, a singing voice for the youthful hero), which concern the stage, not the film genre.
gothic_horror.source: Paul Ranger (excerpted), Performing Arts and the Gothic (excerpting Paul Ranger, 'Terror and Pity Reign in Every Breast': Gothic Drama in the London Patent Theatres, 1750-1820, 1991) (Encyclopedia.com (Gothic Literature reference), 1991 (excerpt)), https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/culture-magazines/performing-arts-and-gothic [read directly]; Peter Hutchings, Hammer and Beyond: The British Horror Film (Manchester University Press, 1993), https://books.google.com/books/about/Hammer_and_beyond.html?id=_HxZAAAAMAAJ [from a search summary]
