gothic_horror.sourceSupports: Performing Arts and the Gothic (excerpting Paul Ranger, 'Terror and Pity Reign in Every Breast': Gothic Drama in the London Patent Theatres, 1750-1820, 1991): On the Gothic stage, 'a singing voice was a requisite for the part of the youthful hero' and older tragic roles needed 'a sturdy figure and a bass voice through which a range of disturbed passions could be expressed'. On reading the page, it doesn’t describe a declamatory style as such, and says nothing about film. Hammer and Beyond: The British Horror Film: Its title and author were verified as the standard scholarly study of Hammer gothic; no passage on acting style was found in what could be read. It’s cited only to record that the search reached scholarship and found nothing on performance.
gothic_horror.how: one of its two sources read directly and the other from a search summary, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: unsupported: The only scholarly source is about 18th-19th-century stage Gothic and, on reading, records casting requirements rather than a heightened delivery. Claims that Hammer films were 'theatrical' or 'melodramatic' came only from fan sites and Wikipedia, and none concern heightened language (verse, rhetoric), which is what the tag means.

gothic_horror.uncertainty: The earlier claim overstated the Ranger excerpt. Hutchings’s book may discuss performance, but couldn’t be read. If anything, the theatrical style belongs to British horror drawn from stage melodrama (Tod Slaughter, Hammer), which is unsourced here.

grindhouse.claim: Grindhouse-style films have prized performers who do their own stunts, for the gut reaction of visibly real action, alongside the speed and lurid content of the exploitation films they imitate.
grindhouse.source: Rotten Tomatoes, 'Zoe Bell talks Death Proof with RT' — https://editorial.rottentomatoes.com/article/zoe-bell-talks-death-proof-with-rt; Eric Schaefer, 'Exploitation Films', Schirmer Encyclopedia of Film — https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/exploitation-films
grindhouse.sourceSupports: Bell: doing her own stunts 'was like a stipulation! ... he said, "That’s part of the reason I’m casting you"'; an actor doing her own stunts gives 'a gut reaction, a sense of reality'. Schaefer: exploitation shoots were 'less than a week', with 'stilted performances' and gore spectacle.

tags.why: Bell, cast in Death Proof (half of the 2007 Grindhouse), says doing her own stunts was a condition of the casting.

grindhouse.uncertainty: Death Proof is a homage, and Bell is a stuntwoman by trade; nothing shows the original grindhouse circuit’s films used stunts the actors performed. 'Without retakes' is unsourced. On review (October 10, 2026), a homage and a stuntwoman by trade weren’t enough to make it a requirement of the whole genre.

hangout.claim: The hangout film, a term Tarantino coined for Rio Bravo, favors character and vibe over plot, so the audience spends time with characters who feel like friends. No credible source makes naturalistic acting a convention of the whole form; naturalism belongs to Linklater-style and mumblecore-adjacent films.
hangout.source: Chris Forrester, Howard Hawks, Rio Bravo, and the Hangout Film (Establishing Shot (Indiana University blog), 2024), https://blogs.iu.edu/establishingshot/2024/06/10/howard-hawks-rio-bravo-and-the-hangout-film/ [read directly]; Dennis Lim, A Generation Finds Its Mumble (The New York Times, 2007), https://www.indiewire.com/2007/08/nyt-a-generation-finds-its-mumble-74060/ [from a search summary]; BFI, Dazed and Confused: how Richard Linklater created the ultimate high-school experience (BFI on Letterboxd), https://letterboxd.com/bfi/story/dazed-and-confused-how-richard-linklater/ [from a search summary]
hangout.sourceSupports: Howard Hawks, Rio Bravo, and the Hangout Film: The hangout film prioritizes 'vibe and character over pure narrative momentum'; Rio Bravo 'is the film in reference to which Quentin Tarantino coined the term'. It says nothing about naturalistic acting; its exemplar is a 1959 studio western. A Generation Finds Its Mumble: Mumblecore deals with nonprofessional actors and quasi-improvised dialogue; narratives 'hinge less on plot points than on the tipping points in interpersonal relationships'. It’s about mumblecore, a related but distinct form. Dazed and Confused: how Richard Linklater created the ultimate high-school experience: The page couldn’t be opened again. An earlier search summary: Linklater’s emphasis on naturalistic dialogue and cast chemistry. That’s one director.
hangout.how: one of its three sources read directly and the other two from search summaries, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: subgenre-or-role: Naturalistic, low-key screen acting is documented only for Linklater’s films and mumblecore. The genre’s defining source (Tarantino via Rio Bravo) is about time with characters, and its exemplar isn’t a naturalistic film.

hangout.uncertainty: The hangout film is a critic’s category, not an established genre with a scholarly literature. Chemistry is emphasized in listicles, but none of the requirements the game can ask for covers it.
hangout.belongsTo: Linklater-style and mumblecore-adjacent naturalistic hangout films

heist.claim: Heist films are built around a crew of specialists, each with one skill, so each actor must establish a distinct role within an ensemble.
heist.source: MasterClass, 'Heist Movie Genre' — https://www.masterclass.com/articles/heist-movies-guide (couldn’t be opened; from a search summary)
heist.sourceSupports: From search summaries: heist films include the assembly of the crew, 'disparate individual criminals, each with their own set of unique skills', each 'the best at their particular skill: safe-cracking, security system disabling, driving fast getaway vehicles'.
heist.uncertainty: The source describes the narrative structure, not what it asks of actors; 'ensemble precision and cool, controlled tension' is unsourced. No interviews on heist-film acting were found.

historical_drama.claim: Period drama asks actors for period-accurate speech: British productions want a period form of Received Pronunciation, not the modern one.
historical_drama.source: Chris Lang (dialect coach), 'British RP Accent for Actors: What You Actually Need to Know' — https://www.dialectcoachchrislang.com/articles/british-rp-accent-for-actors
historical_drama.sourceSupports: 'There’s antique RP for period pieces. There’s mid-century RP for postwar dramas'; 'An actor who learns one version and applies it to everything will sound off target in half their roles'; for British content 'the bar for authenticity is high.'

tags.why: A working dialect coach says period pieces call for a specific period accent (antique RP) that actors must learn.

historical_drama.uncertainty: This is a practitioner’s article about British productions only. Portraying real historical figures, and period manners or bearing, are unsourced here (see the Docudrama genre for portraying real people). On review (October 10, 2026), one practitioner’s article about British productions wasn’t enough to make it a requirement of the whole genre.
historical_drama.belongsTo: British period productions that ask for period Received Pronunciation

historical_fiction.claim: A leading drama school teaches period movement as the etiquette of a period, including deportment and dance, and one period series sent its leads to dance, voice and etiquette lessons. No credible source says period fiction as a whole asks actors for dance or for heightened language.
historical_fiction.source: Royal Academy of Dramatic Art (taught by Francine Watson Coleman), Period Movement for Actors (short course) (RADA, n.d.), https://www.rada.ac.uk/short-courses/period-movement-actors/ [read directly]; Casting Frontier blog, Epic Actor Training for the Bridgerton Series (Casting Frontier, 2021), https://castingfrontier.com/blog/epic-actor-training-for-the-bridgerton-series/ [read directly]
historical_fiction.sourceSupports: Period Movement for Actors (short course): It examines "principles and rules of behaviour in three key periods of western social history, including deportment, greetings, social interaction, clothing, and dance"; units on Elizabethan/Jacobean court behavior (Shakespeare), Restoration comedy, and the 1920s Charleston. It’s training for period work generally, chiefly for the theater. Epic Actor Training for the Bridgerton Series: "Dynevor and Page attended dancing, voice, and etiquette lessons. Altogether, the duo learned how to talk, sit, eat, and walk like 1800's upper-class society." That’s one series.
historical_fiction.how: both its sources read directly, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: subgenre-or-role: RADA treats period dance as part of period-movement training, and Bridgerton’s leads learned ballroom dance, but both concern material with social-dance scenes (court, Regency and costume-romance settings), not historical fiction as a whole, which also covers war, ancient-world and other stories without dance.

subgenre-or-role: Heightened language (verse, rhetoric) belongs to period texts such as Shakespeare and Restoration comedy, which RADA’s course names. Voice and etiquette lessons for a period drama in modern prose are speech and manners, closer to accent work than to heightened language. No credible source makes it a convention of historical fiction.

historical_fiction.uncertainty: The only film-specific source is a casting-platform blog about one deliberately anachronistic series. A trade article on period acting (Backstage, 'What is a Period Piece?') couldn’t be opened, and wasn’t read. The convention of period Received Pronunciation, if it’s real, would be a matter for Accents, not Heightened Language.
historical_fiction.belongsTo: period stories with social-dance scenes (court, Regency, costume romance) for Dancing, and to adaptations of period plays (Shakespeare, Restoration comedy) or scripts written in period verse or rhetoric for Heightened Language

holiday.claim: Holiday films, the Hallmark kind especially, ask actors to play sentimental material with total sincerity rather than irony.
holiday.source: Backstage, '12 Heartwarming Hallmark Holiday Films + What Actors Can Learn From Embracing the Cheese' — https://www.backstage.com/magazine/article/best-hallmark-christmas-movies-78065/ (from a search summary)
holiday.sourceSupports: From search summaries: 'Behind every Hallmark holiday movie lies surprising craft and skillful sincerity'; actors should 'maintain complete sincerity and earnestness, especially when delivering lines about Christmas magic' and deliver 'every cutesy holiday metaphor like they absolutely mean it.'
holiday.uncertainty: The article wasn’t read directly; it covers Hallmark’s formula, not holiday film in general. Sincerity isn’t one of the requirements the game can ask for. No source shows comic timing as something the genre asks, so the research didn’t name Comic Timing.

hood_film.claim: The 'hood film is tied to hip-hop culture and casts rappers-turned-actors; the founding film cast many inexperienced local actors for authenticity.
hood_film.source: 'The Geography of Melodrama, The Melodrama of Geography: The 'Hood Film's Spatial Pathos', Cinephile vol. 4 — http://cinephile.ca/archives/volume-4-post-genre/the-geography-of-melodrama-the-melodrama-of-geography-the-hood-films-spatial-pathos/ (the site’s certificate failed; from a search summary); Wikipedia, 'Hood film' (pointer only)
hood_film.sourceSupports: From a search summary: the 'hood film is identified 'by a strong connection to youth rap/hip hop culture (via soundtrack and rappers-turned-actors), contemporary urban settings ... and inner-city social and political issues'; it builds on Paula J. Massood’s Black City Cinema. Search summaries of Grokipedia, which is unreliable and wasn’t used for a requirement, say Singleton cast 'mostly inexperienced actors' and drew on vernacular speech.
hood_film.uncertainty: No credible source states a performance demand. Vernacular speech appears only in unreliable sources, so the research didn’t name Accents. Rappers-turned-actors is a casting pattern, not a skill.

horror.claim: Horror asks actors for sustained physical exertion (running, crawling, struggling, some fight work), extreme vocal work such as screaming, and believable reactions to threats that are often absent or minimal on set.
horror.source: Frazer Shepherdson, 'A Comprehensive Guide to Acting in Horror Movies', StageMilk (July 16, 2024), https://www.stagemilk.com/a-comprehensive-guide-to-acting-in-horror-movies/
horror.sourceSupports: "The amount of running, crawling and struggling in horror films is unparalleled"; actors work in "extreme vocal ranges: screaming, growling, shouting and crying"; stage combat familiarity helps since "you will have some instruction...but it helps to be familiar with the base concepts"; actors must imagine, for example, "a shapeshifting demon crawling towards you down a hallway" when effects are minimal or absent. Search summaries (the Mandy and Backstage pages couldn’t be opened) also quote Maika Monroe: "the screaming and crying and running...every day is very tiresome."

tags.why: StageMilk says the running, crawling and struggling in horror is 'unparalleled' and recommends stage combat grounding because fight instruction on set is limited.

horror.uncertainty: StageMilk is an acting-advice site written by practitioners, not a textbook or a union source. Screaming is vocal stamina, which isn’t one of the requirements the game can ask for. The research didn’t name Voice-Led Performance, because the source is about screaming on camera, not performing with the voice alone. The Mandy, StarNow and Backstage articles on horror acting couldn’t be opened, and weren’t read. On review (October 10, 2026), one advice site generalizing exertion and some fight work to all horror wasn’t enough to make it a requirement of the whole genre.
horror.belongsTo: chase-and-struggle roles (see the Slasher genre’s final girl)

horror_comedy.claim: Horror comedy asks actors to play the horror element completely straight while the comedy comes from character and situation, so the cast must hold comic timing without winking at the threat.
horror_comedy.source: 'Shaun of the Dead: An Interview with Simon Pegg', BlackFilm.com (September 17, 2004), http://www.blackfilm.com/20040917/features/simonpegg.shtml
horror_comedy.sourceSupports: Pegg: "the zombie element is completely true, and we don’t ever - they’re never comic"; "the zombie element itself is done with reverence and good faith"; the film isn’t a parody but "like another film has crashed into a romantic comedy", with the romantic-comedy side being what is sent up.

tags.why: Pegg describes the film as a romantic comedy colliding with a zombie film; the comedy (not the horror) is where the comic register sits. The genre’s cited definition calls for comedy too.

horror_comedy.uncertainty: These are one film’s makers speaking about their own approach; generalizing 'play the horror straight' to the whole genre is an inference. Other horror comedies, splatter comedies for one, may play the gore for laughs. The IndieWire oral history was behind a paywall, and wasn’t read.

isekai.claim: Isekai is predominantly an anime and light-novel form, so the screen performer is usually a voice actor, who may have to voice a modern adult’s interior life inside a fantastical new body.
isekai.sourceSupports: Okasaki, voice of Rimuru in That Time I Got Reincarnated as a Slime, says the challenge "was definitely to find that cute voice in expression, while at the same time making sure that 37 years of middle-aged experience came through behind the voice." The genre definition (Wikipedia, used only as a lead) lists isekai as a subgenre of 'Japanese light novels, video games, manga, and anime'.

tags.why: The cited performer’s isekai role is voice-only animation voicing, and she describes the vocal problem of the role directly.

isekai.uncertainty: This is one interview about one role. Live-action isekai exists but wasn’t researched. The 'comic asides' of the earlier research aren’t supported by anything found.

jukebox_musical.claim: A jukebox musical asks actors to sing well-known popular songs as character, and in biographical cases performers report deliberately avoiding impersonation of the original artist.
jukebox_musical.source: Penn State News, 'I am woman: Sarah Bockel' (Bockel on playing Carole King in Beautiful), https://www.psu.edu/news/arts-and-entertainment/story/i-am-woman-sarah-bockel
jukebox_musical.sourceSupports: Bockel: "I’m not playing her as a person because this is a musicalized version"; she set aside YouTube research on King to avoid seeming like an impersonation; "I’m just myself with an accent." A critic quoted says she "sings with an appealing and versatile voice that echoes King’s own soulful vocals without straying into mimicry." Its definition (from search summaries of Wikipedia and dictionaries): a stage musical or film whose featured songs are mostly already well-known popular songs.

tags.why: It follows from the cited definition (a musical built on popular songs), and from Bockel’s account of singing King’s songs without mimicry.

jukebox_musical.uncertainty: Dance isn’t supported by anything found, though many jukebox musicals include it. A search summary reports Jessie Mueller saying Beautiful isn’t a jukebox musical, so the example’s classification is contested. The 'accent' Bockel mentions belongs to a biographical role, and doesn’t make Accents a requirement of the genre.

kitchen_sink.claim: Kitchen sink films of the British New Wave cast unknown regional actors and kept broad regional accents intact, breaking with earlier British films whose characters spoke in the accents of the educated London classes.
kitchen_sink.source: Neil Mitchell, Where to begin with kitchen sink drama (BFI, 2016), https://www.bfi.org.uk/features/where-begin-with-kitchen-sink-drama [read directly]; David Hanley, The British New Wave and Its Sources (Offscreen, vol. 15 no. 6, 2011), https://offscreen.com/view/british_new_wave [read directly]
kitchen_sink.sourceSupports: Where to begin with kitchen sink drama: The films 'were predominantly focused on the lives of the working classes, with broad regional accents thankfully intact', and gave us 'some of the greatest performances and most searing dialogue yet seen in British cinema'. The British New Wave and Its Sources: The New Wave opposed mainstream British film by 'opting for location shooting and the employment of unknown regional actors' (citing John Hill), where before 'almost all characters were from London and spoke in the accents of the educated classes'; Saturday Night and Sunday Morning opens with Arthur greeting the audience 'in the accents of industrial Nottinghamshire'.
kitchen_sink.how: both its sources read directly, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: Two independent, credible sources (BFI, and Hanley building on John Hill’s scholarship) state that regional accents and regional actors were a defining convention of the cycle as a whole, not of one film.

kitchen_sink.uncertainty: The sources describe regional speech as a convention, often met by casting actors with those accents rather than by accent technique. The claim that the form asked for a new naturalistic acting style wasn’t sourced beyond search summaries, and is left out.

legal_drama.claim: Legal drama is reputed to ask actors for memorized, persuasive courtroom speeches such as closing arguments, but no performer or teacher source stating this was read.
legal_drama.source: Backstage, 'Playing Lawyers', https://www.backstage.com/magazine/article/playing-lawyers-56452/ (couldn’t be opened; seen only in search results)
legal_drama.sourceSupports: From search summaries only: Paul Newman’s closing argument in The Verdict is described as 'moving, memorized and authentic' and is often referenced for actors learning to play lawyers; Gregory Peck’s closing in To Kill a Mockingbird uses 'pauses and silence as effectively as he uses words.' The summaries don’t say which page each line came from.
legal_drama.uncertainty: No page was read. No source found supports 'technical' jargon delivery as a genre demand. None of the requirements the game can ask for fits speechmaking.

magical_realism.claim: Magic realism as a narrative mode presents fantastic elements in a matter-of-fact way within realistic fiction. No credible source found states that this translates into a particular acting register for film.
magical_realism.source: The Editors of Encyclopaedia Britannica, Magic realism (Encyclopaedia Britannica), https://www.britannica.com/art/magic-realism [from a search summary]; Simon X., assessed essay: representing trauma in magical realist cinema (Medium), https://medium.com/@SimonXIX/magical-realism-essay-954e1cf7c205 [from a search summary]
magical_realism.sourceSupports: Magic realism: Magic realism is a narrative strategy characterized by 'the matter-of-fact inclusion of fantastic or mythical elements into seemingly realistic fiction'. It’s literary, not about acting. assessed essay: representing trauma in magical realist cinema: A student essay, which couldn’t be opened: directors have actors act in a 'natural, laid-back way' without shock at the magic. It isn’t a credible source.
magical_realism.how: neither of its sources read directly, both from search summaries, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: unsupported: The matter-of-fact convention is credibly established for literary narration only. Its transfer to screen acting rests on a student essay and blog posts (e.g. a Volver example), none credible.

magical_realism.uncertainty: A Buffalo State thesis on magical realist film turned up but couldn’t be opened. The inference that matter-of-fact narration implies naturalistic acting is plausible but unsourced.

medical_drama.claim: Medical drama asks actors to learn convincing procedural business (suturing, auscultation, intubation) and to master dense medical jargon, typically through a pre-production medical boot camp and drilled repetition.
medical_drama.source: E! Online, 'The New Grey's Anatomy Cast Explains the Doctor "Boot Camp" They Had to Go Through', https://www.eonline.com/news/1349341/the-new-greys-anatomy-cast-explains-the-doctor-boot-camp-they-had-to-go-through
medical_drama.sourceSupports: Adelaide Kane: the newcomers "started out with a two week boot camp"; "They taught us how to suture and how to check heartbeats... how to listen for breath sounds and how to intubate people." Harry Shum Jr. on jargon: the approach was "repetition"; "We stumble a lot."
medical_drama.uncertainty: This is one show’s practice. None of the requirements the game can ask for covers technical jargon or procedural business, so none applies. 'High-stakes emotion', from the earlier research, isn’t addressed by the source.

military.claim: Military and war films commonly put actors through a pre-shoot boot camp run by a military adviser, covering weapons handling, gear, squad tactics and physical hardship, to make soldiering second nature.
military.source: Aaron Kassraie, 'Dale Dye: Hollywood's Go-To Military Advisor', AARP, https://www.aarp.org/veterans/hollywood-film-industry-military-adviser/
military.sourceSupports: Ron Livingston: the camp included "weapons training, how to handle military gear and other squad-based tactics" that needed to "become second nature"; Dye allowed "up to two hours of sleep a night and two meals a day"; Dye: he "breaks actors down and builds them back up." Search summaries of Variety (not opened) add that Saving Private Ryan’s cast did 10 days of pre-dawn reveille, five-mile runs and weapons training.

tags.why: The boot camps described are sustained physical training with weapons and squad tactics for combat scenes; note this is firearms and tactics, not choreographed fight work.

military.uncertainty: The evidence is from one adviser’s films (the era of Platoon, Saving Private Ryan and Band of Brothers); peacetime 'military life' films without combat weren’t researched. Drill and bearing as such aren’t named in the source that was read. On review (October 10, 2026), one adviser’s films weren’t enough to make it a requirement of the whole genre.
military.belongsTo: combat films with an adviser’s boot camp (see the War genre)

monster_movie.claim: Monster movies have a tradition of the creature itself being played by a performer in a suit, which demands heavy physical endurance and studied non-human movement.
monster_movie.source: Haruo Nakajima interview, 'MR. GODZILLA SPEAKS!', Vantage Point Interviews (May 18, 2017), https://vantagepointinterviews.com/2017/05/18/mr-godzilla-speaks-suit-actor-haruo-nakajima-on-playing-the-king-of-the-monsters/; Dartmouth Library, 'Monsters in motion pictures', https://researchguides.dartmouth.edu/filmgenres/monsters
monster_movie.sourceSupports: Nakajima: "the temperature of my suits reached 60 degrees Celsius"; the 1954 suit weighed about 100 kg; "I watched the movement of bears"; "you cannot complain because you are a professional actor; you have to act like there is no pain." The Dartmouth guide notes Godzilla as "actor Haruo Nakajima in a rubber suit" and classes monster movies as a horror subgenre (Oxford Dictionary of Film Studies).

tags.why: Nakajima describes performing a creature in a heavy suit and building its movement from animal study; the Dartmouth guide names suit performance as the tokusatsu foundation of the genre.

monster_movie.uncertainty: It covers the creature performer, not the human leads. The earlier claim about reacting to a creature added later in effects was supported only by search summaries about other kinds of film (Casper, Hobbit), and isn’t used. Suit work is one tradition (kaiju); many modern monster films use CGI. On review (October 10, 2026), a demand on the creature performer alone wasn’t enough to make it a requirement of the whole genre.
monster_movie.belongsTo: the performer in the creature suit

mystery.claim: A source on a modern whodunit says the form wants heightened, larger-than-life suspects who still read as real people; nothing found supports a distinct technique for withholding secrets.
mystery.source: SlashFilm, ''Knives Out' Director Rian Johnson And Star Michael Shannon On Blending Comedy With Mystery...', https://www.slashfilm.com/570824/knives-out-interview/
mystery.sourceSupports: Johnson: "you need to get great actors and actors who can do performances that are this big but still feel like real people." He also says "all of the funniest lines in the movie, Michael just shouted out on the day." A separate search summary (Screen Rant, not opened) says Johnson gives actors the full script including the killer’s identity.
mystery.uncertainty: This is one director on one comic whodunit. No source found says what mystery asks of actors generally; 'withholding and layering' remains an unsourced reading. Shannon’s ad-libs don’t establish improvisation as a convention of the form.

neo_noir.claim: Film reference works name first-person voice-over narration as a convention of classic film noir. No credible source found says neo-noir keeps it as a convention; neo-noir is described by its self-consciousness and nostalgia for noir, and many neo-noirs have no narrator.
neo_noir.source: Dartmouth College Library, Film noir (research guide, quoting A Dictionary of Film Studies, Kuhn and Westwell, Oxford, 2020) (Dartmouth Library Research Guides, n.d.), https://researchguides.dartmouth.edu/filmgenres/noir [read directly]; William Luhr, Film Noir (Schirmer Encyclopedia of Film, via Encyclopedia.com, 2007), https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/film-noir [read directly]
neo_noir.sourceSupports: Film noir (research guide, quoting A Dictionary of Film Studies, Kuhn and Westwell, Oxford, 2020): It quotes Kuhn and Westwell: noir is a cycle of 1940-1959 Hollywood crime films with "dreamlike first-person voice-over narration, flashbacks, temporal ellipses, and often ambiguous endings." It gives no definition of neo-noir. Film Noir: It uses Double Indemnity’s narrator voice-over as an example of classic noir, and says "neo-noir films display a self-consciousness alien to earlier ones" and a "conflicted nostalgia" for the postwar era. It says nothing on voice-over in neo-noir.
neo_noir.how: both its sources read directly, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: subgenre-or-role: Voice-over narration is sourced as a classic-noir convention only. For neo-noir it belongs to the narrator role in those films that keep it (retro neo-noir pastiches and narrated films), not to the genre.

neo_noir.uncertainty: No source about neo-noir performance was found. Andrew Spicer (Film Noir, Longman, 2002) was seen only through a summary noting that noir devices such as voice-over appear in non-noir films too. 'Deadpan' delivery, 'cool understatement' and 'controlled menace' remain unsupported.
neo_noir.belongsTo: the narrating lead in neo-noirs that keep classic noir’s first-person voice-over

nordic_noir.claim: The best-known Nordic noir lead describes a performance built from tight control of a closed, socially difficult character; the genre is characterized as slow and melancholic, but nothing found ties a specific acting style to the genre.
nordic_noir.source: Barry Forshaw, 'SOFIA ON SAGA: Sofia Helin talks Saga Norén and The Bridge', Crime Time, https://www.crimetime.co.uk/sofia-on-saga-sofia-helin-talks-saga-noren-and-the-bridge-to-barry-forshaw/
nordic_noir.sourceSupports: Helin: "At first I regarded her as a blank wall, but then that blank wall became a glass wall and I was able to see through it"; she chose to make it look like Saga "was forcing herself to do eye contact"; "I usually have to keep Saga within certain parameters." Search summaries (of genre sites, not opened) describe Nordic noir’s "slow and melancholic pace".
nordic_noir.uncertainty: This is one character in one series; Saga’s restraint is a character trait, not evidence of a style across the genre. No scholarly source on Nordic noir performance was found. Bilingual productions (The Bridge) suggest language demands but no source said so.

occult.claim: Possession and exorcism films have asked for extreme vocal and makeup work for the possessed role, as in The Exorcist, where a separate voice actress (Mercedes McCambridge) built the demon’s voice under punishing conditions and the possessed actress wore prosthetics applied for hours daily. These are role-specific to possession films, not conventions of occult horror.
occult.source: Jacob Slankard, The Actor Behind the Demon's Voice in The Exorcist Went to Hell and Back (Collider, 2023), https://collider.com/the-exorcist-demon-voice-mercedes-mccambridge/ [read directly]; Looper (byline not verified), Why Linda Blair Was Never The Same After The Exorcist (Looper, unknown), https://www.looper.com/171562/why-linda-blair-was-never-the-same-after-the-exorcist/ [from a search summary]
occult.sourceSupports: The Actor Behind the Demon’s Voice in The Exorcist Went to Hell and Back: McCambridge voiced the demon, insisting on 'being tightly bound to a chair, swallowing raw eggs and Jack Daniel’s while smoking'; Friedkin layered the recordings. The article doesn’t mention Linda Blair’s makeup. Why Linda Blair Was Never The Same After The Exorcist: Blair spent at least two hours, sometimes up to five, in the makeup chair daily for Dick Smith’s prosthetics. It’s an entertainment site of little authority, read only as a search summary.
occult.how: one of its two sources read directly and the other from a search summary, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: subgenre-or-role: Documented for one film’s demon voice, performed by a separate voice actor. It belongs to the possessing-entity role in possession films, not to occult horror generally.

subgenre-or-role: Prosthetic makeup for the possessed character is snippet-only and from one film; it belongs to the possessed role in possession/exorcism films. Makeup is applied by the effects team, so it is an endurance demand more than an acting technique.

occult.uncertainty: It’s a single film. Searches for a source describing possession-film acting as a convention returned only listicles. Occult horror also covers witchcraft, cults and séance films with no possession role.
occult.belongsTo: the possessed role, and the voice of the possessing entity, in possession and exorcism films

parody.claim: Screen parody of the Airplane! school asks actors to deliver absurd material with complete dramatic seriousness, deadpan, oblivious to the gags around them.
parody.sourceSupports: Nielsen could invest "the most ridiculous lines of dialogue with a delivery that was serious as a heart attack"; the Zucker-Abrahams-Zucker team cast him as "an archetypal straight man oblivious to the constant stream of gags going on around him." A search summary of Nielsen’s 1993 Fresh Air interview (NPR; the page didn’t load): approaching the material "with the same seriousness and the same gravity" as their police shows "would be very funny."

tags.why: The A.V. Club credits the comedy to Nielsen’s deadpan delivery of ridiculous lines, which is verbal comic timing played straight.

parody.uncertainty: This is one school of parody, Zucker-Abrahams-Zucker’s. Parody that relies on mimicry of a specific performer (sketch parody) wasn’t researched. 'Precise imitation of a recognisable style' isn’t directly supported.

picaresque.claim: The model screen picaresque was carried by its lead’s charm across an episodic, roistering narrative; nothing found generalizes this into a performance demand.
picaresque.source: Criterion Collection, 'Tom Jones (1963)', https://www.criterion.com/films/28736-tom-jones (couldn’t be opened; seen in a search summary)
picaresque.sourceSupports: From a search summary: Tom Jones is "a spirited picaresque"; "Albert Finney gives a career-defining performance as the foundling whose easy charm seems to lead him astray at every turn." Another search summary (its source unclear) mentions "asides to the screen."
picaresque.uncertainty: It’s one film, from a search summary only. There’s no source on what picaresque asks of actors generally. 'Shifting register across settings' is unsupported. The 'asides to the screen' line couldn’t be attributed, and wasn’t used for a requirement.

police_procedural.claim: Police procedurals train their casts in real procedure (classroom instruction, traffic stops, cuffing, clearing a house, defensive tactics, ride-alongs) so the actions read as second nature on camera.
police_procedural.source: Michael Cudlitz, 'Ride-Along (I'm Not a Cop, But I Look Like One on TV)', HuffPost, https://www.huffpost.com/entry/southland-preview_b_1211491
police_procedural.sourceSupports: Cudlitz (who played John Cooper on Southland): "We started in a classroom covering many of the things we would be required to do on film as cops"; training covered car positioning at traffic stops, cuffing, clearing a house and defensive tactics, ending in a ride-along with an on-duty officer; the aim was for procedure to become "second nature."
police_procedural.uncertainty: This is one show, in an article by one of its actors. Defensive tactics are mentioned, but not as sustained fight work, so Fights And Stunts doesn’t apply. 'Restraint in interrogation' is unsupported. None of the requirements the game can ask for covers fluency in procedure.

political_drama.claim: Political drama in the Sorkin mold asks actors to master fast, dense, exact dialogue through heavy repetition so it becomes subconscious, often delivered on the move.
political_drama.source: Screen Rant, 'The West Wing's Bradley Whitford Explains Aaron Sorkin's Speedy Dialogue', https://screenrant.com/bradley-whitford-west-wing-aaron-sorkin-dialogue/
political_drama.sourceSupports: Whitford: actors must "learn your lines as fast as you can" and do "endless repetitions" to make dialogue "subconscious, so that technical aspect of the performance was removed"; Sorkin writes "racing, like, just ahead of the audience." A search summary (Cheat Sheet, not opened): Martin Sheen said actors could suggest but not improvise, and Sorkin wanted lines verbatim because he wrote 'in meter'.
political_drama.uncertainty: This is one writer’s style on one show, not the genre. Heightened Language was considered (the 'meter' claim), but that rests on a search summary and on one writer, so the research didn’t name it. 'Quiet calculation of characters wielding power' is unsupported.

political_thriller.claim: A leading conspiracy-thriller performance was built on stillness and near-invisibility rather than display; nothing found makes this a stated genre convention.
political_thriller.source: The Film Stage, 'Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy Star Gary Oldman Talks His Subtle Performance...', https://thefilmstage.com/interview-tinker-tailor-soldier-spy-star-gary-oldman-talks-his-subtle-performance-james-bond-more/
political_thriller.sourceSupports: Oldman cites le Carré’s description of Smiley as a "swift" that can regulate its temperature to the room, "Almost like a chameleon", and says that passage "was where the stillness comes from"; he and Tomas Alfredson avoided details that would make Smiley memorable.
political_thriller.uncertainty: Tinker Tailor is usually classed as a spy thriller, so it’s a neighboring example, not a clean political-thriller one. Oldman doesn’t use the words paranoia or restraint. No source on the genre as a whole was found.

post_apocalyptic.claim: Leads in two post-apocalyptic films lost around 30 pounds for survival-worn looks (Hardy, Mad Max: Fury Road; Mortensen, The Road), and Hardy planned months of daily fight training. These are particular productions, not genre conventions.
post_apocalyptic.source: Steven Weintraub, Tom Hardy Interview MAD MAX: FURY ROAD; Training, His Look, Shooting Schedule, Filming with George Miller (Collider, 2010), https://collider.com/tom-hardy-interview-mad-max-fury-road-training-look-shooting-schedule-filming-george-miller/ [read directly]; Sheila Roberts, Viggo Mortensen Interview THE ROAD (Collider, 2009), https://collider.com/viggo-mortensen-interview-the-road/ [read directly]
post_apocalyptic.sourceSupports: Tom Hardy Interview MAD MAX: FURY ROAD; Training, His Look, Shooting Schedule, Filming with George Miller: Hardy: 'I’m meant to drop 30 pounds... I’ve already dropped it'; 'I’ll probably get three or four months of fight training out there. Seven days a week.' Viggo Mortensen Interview THE ROAD: Mortensen: 'from the clothes that didn’t fit, I think it was around maybe 30 pounds'; 'I just ate a lot less.'
post_apocalyptic.how: both its sources read directly, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: subgenre-or-role: Fight training is documented only for Fury Road, an action-led entry. Many post-apocalyptic films (The Road) aren’t combat-driven; no source states combat as a genre-wide demand on actors.
subgenre-or-role: Weight loss is documented for two leads playing starving survivors. It belongs to those roles; no source states it as a genre convention.

post_apocalyptic.uncertainty: Searches for genre conventions found only student slides and listicles (wasteland settings, scavenging, survival), nothing credible on what the genre asks of actors. The 'little dialogue' claim about Fury Road stays unconfirmed.
post_apocalyptic.belongsTo: action-led post-apocalyptic films (the Mad Max line) for Fights And Stunts, and to particular leads playing starving survivors for Physical Transformation

prison_film.claim: Some prison films build performance from authenticity: casting formerly incarcerated people and shooting improvised, documentary-feel ensemble scenes, or shooting in real former prisons.
prison_film.source: ABC News (Australia), 'Sing Sing tells a remarkable true story of a prison theatre program, starring Colman Domingo' (January 14, 2025), https://www.abc.net.au/news/2025-01-14/sing-sing-colman-domingo-interview/104791974
prison_film.sourceSupports: "More than 85 per cent of Sing Sing’s cast is made up of formerly incarcerated men playing versions of themselves"; rehearsal scenes were "largely improvised and shot via Steadicam, giving them a documentary feel"; the directors "merely provided prompts." Search summaries say Starred Up was shot in a former Belfast prison with ex-convicts.
prison_film.uncertainty: Sing Sing’s method is unusual, so Improvisation isn’t a convention of the genre, and the research didn’t name it. 'Psychological toll of long confinement' is unsupported. No source on the genre as a whole was found.

psychological_horror.claim: A central psychological-horror performance was played as grief and family drama pushed to extremes, with the horror grounded in something real rather than played as spectacle.
psychological_horror.source: Time, 'Toni Collette Interview on New Horror Hit Hereditary', https://time.com/5295637/toni-collette-hereditary-horror-interview/
psychological_horror.sourceSupports: Collette: the film is "a meditation on grief and people dealing with emotional pain"; on intense scenes, "trying to push it away from me until it was the moment between 'action' and 'cut'—resisting it and just letting it out at the right time"; she calls it and The Sixth Sense "not solely horror films."
psychological_horror.uncertainty: It’s one film. No source found states 'subtlety and ambiguity rather than spectacle' as a genre demand; Collette’s performance is in fact very large in places. None of the requirements the game can ask for fits.

psychological_thriller.claim: Psychological thriller leads are often unreliable or self-concealing characters, and one leading example describes playing such a character as clinical and fully worked out in advance.
psychological_thriller.source: Deadline, ''Gone Girl's Rosamund Pike: Portraying The Complicated Amazing Amy' (December 2014), https://deadline.com/2014/12/rosamund-pike-interview-gone-girl-oscars-1201332014/ (behind a paywall; seen in a search summary)
psychological_thriller.sourceSupports: From a search summary: Pike says Amy is "not someone overpowered by rage but driven by rage"; playing her isn’t about unleashing something animal, everything is "worked out in advance," making her "so clinical that it gives the actress a buffer." A separate search summary of NPR’s Fresh Air (Natalie Portman on Black Swan) says she trained with New York City Ballet members.
psychological_thriller.uncertainty: It’s from a search summary only; the page wasn’t read. These are single examples. Ballet in Black Swan belongs to that film, and doesn’t make Dancing a requirement of the genre.

queer_cinema.claim: Queer cinema is defined by its subjects, not by a performance technique; the only performer-side source found concerns intimacy coordination on queer productions.
queer_cinema.source: PinkNews, 'Intimacy co-ordinator behind major queer sex scenes reveals what their job is really like' (October 30, 2024), https://www.thepinknews.com/2024/10/30/queer-intimacy-coordinator-robbie-taylor-hunt-mr-loverman-reverberation/
queer_cinema.sourceSupports: Robbie Taylor Hunt: before rehearsal he asks actors individually "This is what’s in the script, what are we thinking about it? What do we want, and not want, to do?"; his work covers "simulated sex, nudity, kissing, physical touch..." and aims at the scene’s intended emotional and narrative effect.
queer_cinema.uncertainty: Intimacy coordination is general industry practice, not specific to queer cinema, and not every queer film has intimate scenes, so the research didn’t name Staged Intimacy. 'Truthful, unstereotyped portrayal' is unsupported by any source read.

revenge.claim: Revenge action films have required their leads to undergo months of full-time martial-arts and weapons training to carry the fight work.
revenge.source: Collider, ''Kill Bill' Star... Reveals the Grueling Training Sessions', https://collider.com/uma-thurman-kill-bill-training-comments/
revenge.sourceSupports: Thurman trained "three solid months, five days a week, nine to five", learning "knife-throwing, a little bit of target practice. Everything from fencing to samurai style, to Wushu style." Search summaries (Maxim, not opened) say Keanu Reeves trained eight hours a day for six months for John Wick.

tags.why: Thurman describes months of full-time fight and weapons training for the revenge story’s fight sequences.

revenge.uncertainty: Revenge dramas without action, such as slow-burn thrillers, exist and wouldn’t need this. 'Grief turning into obsession' is unsupported. On review (October 10, 2026), training that only revenge action films ask for wasn’t enough to make it a requirement of the whole genre.
revenge.belongsTo: revenge action films and their fight-trained leads

road_movie.claim: The road movie’s in-car filming foregrounds dialogue between side-by-side travelers.
road_movie.source: Kuhn, A. & Westwell, G., 'Road movie', A Dictionary of Film Studies (Oxford University Press, 2020), as quoted on Dartmouth Library's 'Road films' research guide, https://researchguides.dartmouth.edu/filmgenres/roadfilms
road_movie.sourceSupports: "The physical constraints of filming in a car tend to lead to a heavy reliance on side-by-side shots and the foregrounding of dialogue"; road movies also favor "montage sequences, travelling and aerial shots, and diegetic music."
road_movie.uncertainty: The Oxford text was read as quoted by the Dartmouth guide, not in the original. It describes the form’s shooting and dialogue, not what it asks of actors; 'gradual character change' is a narrative feature, not a performance demand. None of the requirements the game can ask for fits.

rockumentary.claim: A rockumentary is a documentary about rock music, so its subjects are real musicians, not actors. Acting demands come from the mock rockumentary: This Is Spinal Tap’s dialogue was, its director says, entirely improvised, and (by secondary report) its leads played and sang the music themselves.
rockumentary.source: Dictionary.com, rockumentary (Dictionary.com, n.d.), https://www.dictionary.com/browse/rockumentary [read directly]; Lou Thomas (interviewer), Rob Reiner: how we made This Is Spinal Tap (BFI, 2022), https://www.bfi.org.uk/interviews/rob-reiner-how-we-made-this-spinal-tap [read directly]; Wikipedia (pointer only), Spinal Tap (band) (Wikipedia, n.d.), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinal_Tap_(band) [read directly]
rockumentary.sourceSupports: rockumentary: "a documentary about rock music"; coined 1970-75 from rock + documentary. Rob Reiner: how we made This Is Spinal Tap: Reiner: "The entire film was improvised. The only speech that’s not improvised is Patrick Macnee." Physical gags (Stonehenge, the amp that goes to 11) were planned; dialogue wasn’t. The page that was read doesn’t quote anyone on the actors playing the music. Spinal Tap (band): "The quintet played their own instruments throughout the film." It’s uncited, and used only as a lead. Search summaries (TCM’s 'Behind the Camera', which couldn’t be opened) say Guest, McKean and Shearer played and sang the music.
rockumentary.how: all three of its sources read directly, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: subgenre-or-role: Improvised dialogue is documented for This Is Spinal Tap, the mock form’s touchstone, by its director. A real rockumentary has no scripted acting at all, so the demand belongs to the mock rockumentary, and the evidence is one film.

subgenre-or-role: In a real rockumentary the singers are the musicians themselves, not actors. Actors singing belongs to the mock rockumentary’s band roles, and even there the evidence is one film and secondary.

rockumentary.uncertainty: The singing claim for Spinal Tap rests on Wikipedia and search summaries; TCM and Britannica couldn’t be opened. Other mock rockumentaries, such as Popstar: Never Stop Never Stopping and CB4, weren’t researched.
rockumentary.belongsTo: the mock rockumentary, This Is Spinal Tap and its imitators, with Improvisation for the whole cast and Singing for the actor-musicians in its band roles

romance.claim: Romance depends on believable chemistry between the leads, which casting tests with paired chemistry reads; nothing authoritative was read.
romance.source: Search summaries only (dictionary-style definition of 'chemistry read', source page not identified); 'Romantic Comedy Acting: Chemistry and Timing', The Playground, https://theplayground.com/romantic-comedy-acting-chemistry-and-timing/ (not opened)
romance.sourceSupports: From a search summary: a chemistry read is "an occasion when actors who are being considered for particular parts... read some of the script together, to see if they work well together and seem to have chemistry." A search summary’s claim that 'over seventy percent of romantic comedy casting decisions are based on chemistry reads' is unsourced, and wasn’t used.
romance.uncertainty: No credible source was read. Staged Intimacy was considered: SAG-AFTRA’s standards for intimacy coordinators (seen only in search summaries; the PDF couldn’t be opened) cover nudity and simulated sex in any genre, not romance as such, so the research didn’t name it.

romantic_drama.claim: A landmark romantic-drama lead described the role as unusually internal, requiring a mature, contained performance of longing; nothing found generalizes this.
romantic_drama.source: PopEntertainment.com, Heath Ledger interview about Brokeback Mountain, http://www.popentertainment.com/ledger.htm (the connection failed; seen in a search summary)
romantic_drama.sourceSupports: From a search summary: Ledger called Ennis "the most complex and internal character" he had been offered and said it would require "a more matured performance."
romantic_drama.uncertainty: It’s from a search summary only, and one film. A search summary claiming Before Sunrise’s dialogue was largely improvised wasn’t used: it’s unattributed, and conflicts with the film being scripted. 'Heightened, sustained emotion... culminating in loss' is unsupported.

satire.claim: In Dr. Strangelove, Peter Sellers played three roles, building each from voice and then walk, and improvised much of his dialogue, which Kubrick kept. This is one film and one performer’s method, not a convention of screen satire.
satire.source: Calum Russell, Peter Sellers' defining performance in 'Dr Strangelove' (Far Out Magazine, 2021), https://faroutmagazine.co.uk/peter-sellers-stanley-kubrick-dr-strangelove/ [read directly]; Wes D. Gehring, Comedy (Schirmer Encyclopedia of Film, via Encyclopedia.com, 2007), https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/comedy [read directly]
satire.sourceSupports: Peter Sellers' defining performance in 'Dr Strangelove': Sellers: 'I start with the voice ... After that I establish how the character walks.' He played Muffley, Mandrake and Strangelove and improvised much of his dialogue, which Kubrick incorporated. Comedy: It distinguishes satire by its corrective aim ('Parody is essentially affectionate in nature, without satire’s goal of offering a corrective to behavior'), and states no acting technique for satire.
satire.how: both its sources read directly, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: subgenre-or-role: Multi-role caricature is documented for Sellers in one film. It belongs to character-comedian satire, not to satire as a form.
subgenre-or-role: Improvisation is documented for Sellers in one film (and is a known feature of character-prank satire such as Borat, from snippets only). No source makes it a convention of satire.

satire.uncertainty: Far Out is a magazine, not a reference work; Britannica’s entry couldn’t be opened. The 'straight face' idea surfaced only from listicles. Satire is defined by aim, not by a performance mode, in the one reference work read.
satire.belongsTo: character-comedian satire (Sellers in Dr. Strangelove) and improvised character-prank satire

science_fantasy.claim: No source was found on what science fantasy specifically asks of an actor. The nearest material is an actor’s account of effects-driven science-fiction work in general.
science_fantasy.source: Stephen Lang interview, Smashing Interviews Magazine, https://smashinginterviews.com/interviews/actors/stephen-lang-interview-avatar-star-on-his-current-role-in-the-fox-sci-fi-series-terra-nova; the genre’s definition: Wikipedia, Science fantasy (pointer only)
science_fantasy.sourceSupports: Lang says that on a green screen 'you really have to use your imagination', and that it demands specificity because you are 'seeing things that are going to be put there later'. None of it is specific to science fantasy as opposed to science fiction.
science_fantasy.uncertainty: There’s no source on this genre in particular. Imagination work on a green screen isn’t one of the requirements the game can ask for. The earlier claim of 'stylised or physical action' is unsourced, and wasn’t carried over into a requirement.

science_fiction.claim: Effects-heavy science fiction asks the actor to play against things that aren’t there, which takes imagination and specificity.
science_fiction.source: Stephen Lang interview, Smashing Interviews Magazine, https://smashinginterviews.com/interviews/actors/stephen-lang-interview-avatar-star-on-his-current-role-in-the-fox-sci-fi-series-terra-nova
science_fiction.sourceSupports: Lang (Avatar, Terra Nova) says green screen 'presents its own challenge', 'you really have to use your imagination', and you are 'seeing things that are going to be put there later'.
science_fiction.uncertainty: This is one actor, read in a search summary. It speaks to effects-driven production, not to science fiction as a genre (much science fiction has no green screen). None of the requirements the game can ask for is work with effects or a green screen, and Naturalism On Camera doesn’t mean that, so the research named none. No source was found on technical exposition.

slapstick.claim: The slapstick comic must be acrobat and stunt performer as well as comedian, with perfect timing.
slapstick.sourceSupports: Quoted in search results as: 'The slapstick comic, more than a mere funnyman or buffoon, must often be an acrobat, a stunt performer, and something of a magician—a master of uninhibited action and perfect timing.' The definition also names broad physical action and roots in commedia dell’arte.

tags.why: Britannica defines slapstick as comedy of broad physical action; the comic is 'a master of uninhibited action'.
Britannica says the slapstick comic 'must often be an acrobat, a stunt performer'.
Britannica names 'perfect timing' as part of the slapstick comic’s mastery.

slapstick.uncertainty: Britannica’s page couldn’t be opened directly; the quotation came back word for word from two separate searches, but wasn’t read on the page. A Scribd copy of the Britannica article also appears in the results.

slasher.claim: Slasher leads, especially the final girl, do physical fight and stunt work in the climactic confrontation, often trained for it, alongside sustained fear.
slasher.source: Fangoria, 'Q&A: Taissa Farmiga Talks The Standout Satirical Slasher THE FINAL GIRLS', https://www.fangoria.com/taissa-farmiga-the-final-girls-interview/; also BuzzFeed, 'The Last Final Girl: How Danielle Harris Survived...', https://www.buzzfeed.com/louispeitzman/from-child-actor-to-scream-queen-how-danielle-harris-became
slasher.sourceSupports: Farmiga: 'I trained for the machete work in the fight scenes, and they had me practice a few times in the harness that would yank me backwards'; filming involved 'a lot of night work and being scared'. Harris (from a search summary): it was 'exhausting fighting these giant guys and kind of having to carry the movie physically as well as emotionally, because the Final Girl has to do both of those things.'

tags.why: Farmiga trained for machete fight work and harness pulls; Harris describes fighting stunt performers as a requirement of the final-girl role.

slasher.uncertainty: Farmiga was read directly; Harris only in a search summary. Both speak about the final-girl lead, not every slasher role. Screaming is described (the scream queen), but it isn’t one of the requirements the game can ask for. The Final Girls is a satirical slasher. On review (October 10, 2026), the final-girl lead alone wasn’t enough to make it a requirement of the whole genre.

slice_of_life.claim: 'Slice of life' comes from Jean Jullien’s naturalist theater (tranche de vie) and names everyday depiction without conventional plot. No source states a naturalistic acting demand for slice-of-life film. Its canonical film master, Ozu, dictated actors’ every gesture, which runs against a naturalistic method.
slice_of_life.source: Ryu Chishu, There was a father: Ryu Chishu remembers Ozu Yasujiro (BFI, Sight and Sound, 1964), https://www.bfi.org.uk/sight-and-sound/interviews/there-was-father-ryu-chishu-remembers-ozu-yasujiro [read directly]; Wikipedia contributors, Slice of life (Wikipedia (pointer only)), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slice_of_life [from a search summary]
slice_of_life.sourceSupports: There was a father: Ryu Chishu remembers Ozu Yasujiro: Ozu 'made up the complete picture in his head before he went on the set'; actors had to 'follow his directions, from the way we lifted and dropped our arms to the way we blinked our eyes'. Slice of life, used only as a lead: the term is a calque of Jullien’s tranche de vie ('A play is a slice of life put onstage with art'); in theater the term refers to naturalism. It’s a storytelling definition, not about acting.
slice_of_life.how: one of its two sources read directly and the other from a search summary, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: unsupported: Only the definition (via Wikipedia) links the form to naturalism, and that is about subject and story. The one acting source found (Ryu on Ozu) describes a precisely dictated style. No credible source makes naturalistic acting a genre demand.

slice_of_life.uncertainty: The theater-naturalism origin is real, but whether that implies an acting technique on film is unsourced. Ozu’s results read as natural on screen, so the counter-evidence is about method, not effect.

space_opera.claim: The term space opera began as a derogatory label for hackneyed pulp spaceship yarns, coined on the model of 'horse opera' and 'soap opera', and the BFI ties the genre to an over-the-top, camp approach to storytelling. Harrison Ford’s on-set joke that Lucas’s Star Wars lines could be typed but not said concerns one film’s dialogue, not heightened or classical language.
space_opera.source: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction (eds. John Clute, David Langford, Graham Sleight), Space Opera (SFE (sf-encyclopedia.com), n.d.), https://sf-encyclopedia.com/entry/space_opera [read directly]; Wang Sum Luk, 10 great space opera films (BFI, 2023), https://www.bfi.org.uk/lists/10-great-space-opera-films [read directly]; SlashFilm, Harrison Ford Wasn't Always A Fan Of George Lucas' Star Wars Writing (SlashFilm, 2023), https://www.slashfilm.com/1110034/harrison-ford-wasnt-always-a-fan-of-george-lucas-star-wars-writing/ [read directly]
space_opera.sourceSupports: Space Opera: Wilson Tucker coined 'space opera' in 1941 for the "hacky, grinding, stinking, outworn, spaceship yarn", after 'horse opera' and 'soap opera'. It says nothing about dialogue or acting in space opera films. 10 great space opera films: Space opera "has long been tied to a silly, over-the-top approach to storytelling"; it cites Sontag on Flash Gordon as camp. It doesn’t discuss dialogue or acting in general terms. Harrison Ford Wasn’t Always A Fan Of George Lucas' Star Wars Writing: Ford’s line "George, you can type this s***, but you can’t say it" was an on-set joke he recounted to GQ in 2017; Lucas told Empire in 1999 that "dialogue isn’t my strength." It says nothing about verse, rhetoric or a classical register.
space_opera.how: all three of its sources read directly, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: unsupported: No credible source says space opera asks actors for heightened or classical language. The 'opera' in the name is a pulp-era insult, not a reference to operatic text; the BFI’s 'over-the-top' is about storytelling and tone. The Star Wars evidence is one franchise’s awkward dialogue, which isn’t verse or rhetoric, and the Lucas 'serial style' quote was only ever seen on a fan site.

space_opera.uncertainty: A broader 'stylised, sincere melodrama' playing style may be real, but it isn’t Heightened Language, and no credible acting source states it. Action and effects work weren’t researched.

spaghetti_western.claim: Leone’s spaghetti westerns hold the actor’s face in extreme close-up with little dialogue; Eastwood played the lead with an economy of words.
spaghetti_western.source: Wikipedia, 'Sergio Leone', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergio_Leone (pointer); Remind Magazine, 'How Did Clint Eastwood Rise to Fame as a Spaghetti Western Antihero?', https://www.remindmagazine.com/article/41352/clint-eastwood-spaghetti-western-antihero-sergio-leone-dollars-trilogy/
spaghetti_western.sourceSupports: Wikipedia (from a search summary): Leone’s style juxtaposes extreme close-ups with long shots; he 'had a fascination with faces and used little dialogue'. Remind (from a search summary): Eastwood wanted to play the Man With No Name 'with an economy of words' and felt 'the less he said, the stronger he became'.

tags.why: The form’s signature is the extreme close-up on a near-silent face, which asks for restrained on-camera playing; Eastwood’s stated choice was minimal speech.

spaghetti_western.uncertainty: One director stands in for the genre. Remind is a popular magazine. Neither source discusses gun or horse handling, which this genre likely shares with the Western. On review (October 10, 2026), one director’s films weren’t enough to make it a requirement of the whole genre.

splatter.claim: No source was found on what splatter asks of the actor specifically. Sources describe effects work and blood rigs rather than performance.
splatter.source: Chicago Reader, 'Behind the gory scenes of Splatter Theater', https://chicagoreader.com/arts-culture/behind-the-gory-scenes-of-splatter-theater/
splatter.sourceSupports: From a search summary: 'wearable gizmos modified to allow performers to disgorge blood on cue' in a stage splatter show. Other results concerned prosthetic makeup in films (The Substance, X) that aren’t clearly splatter.
splatter.uncertainty: The definition centers on special effects, not the actor. The source is about a stage parody. Wearing blood rigs isn’t heavy physical transformation, so the research didn’t name Physical Transformation.

sports.claim: Sports films ask actors to train in the sport depicted so they read as believable athletes.
sports.source: NPR, 'How actors in The Boys in the Boat trained to appear believable as Olympic athletes', https://www.npr.org/2023/12/20/1220558981/how-actors-in-the-boys-in-the-boat-trained-to-appear-believable-as-olympic-athle; The Hollywood Reporter, 'Grading 15 Actors' Sports Skills in Movies', https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/lists/grading-actors-sports-skills-movies/
sports.sourceSupports: NPR’s headline and a search summary: the actors trained to row like the 1936 U.S. Olympic crew in order to 'appear believable as Olympic athletes'. THR grades actors on the sports skill they display on screen.

tags.why: The sources show sustained athletic physical action trained for the role, which the vocabulary’s 'sustained physical action' covers.

sports.uncertainty: The NPR page didn’t load; only its headline and a search summary were read. Fights And Stunts is trained as Stage Combat, which fits combat sports (boxing films) better than rowing or baseball, so the fit is partial. On review (October 10, 2026), a fit with combat sports alone wasn’t enough to make it a requirement of the whole genre.
sports.belongsTo: combat-sport films such as boxing films

spy.claim: No source was found that establishes cover-identity playing or stunt work as a convention of the spy genre for actors.
spy.source: Deadline, 'Keri Russell Is The Russian Next Door In The Americans', https://deadline.com/2014/06/the-offer-to-play-a-russian-spy-came-in-from-the-cold-for-keri-russell-791418/
spy.sourceSupports: In a search summary, Russell says she didn’t focus much on 'the spy stuff' in building Elizabeth Jennings and was more interested in the marriage; she compares the double life to the 'whole other life' every person has.
spy.uncertainty: The one actor source found plays down the spy-specific demand. Accent wasn’t sourced even though the role is a Russian posing as an American. Action-led spy films likely involve stunts, but no source was found.

steampunk.claim: No source was found on what steampunk asks of actors. The sources describe only Victorian-styled costume.
steampunk.sourceSupports: From a search summary: characters typically wear Victorian-era top hats, corsets, petticoats and trench coats.
steampunk.uncertainty: Costume is a design convention, not an acting demand. Period speech wasn’t sourced for steampunk.

stoner_comedy.claim: Stoner comedy is a comedy subgenre centered on cannabis culture, established on screen by Cheech and Chong. Its comic demand follows from its being comedy; no source was found stating an acting demand specific to it.
stoner_comedy.source: Wikipedia contributors, Stoner film (Wikipedia (pointer only), 2026), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoner_film [from a search summary]; Backstage staff (byline not verified), Comedy Terms That Every Actor Should Know (Backstage, unknown), https://www.backstage.com/magazine/article/comedy-terms-every-actor-know-5682/ [from a search summary]
stoner_comedy.sourceSupports: Stoner film, used only as a lead: a subgenre of comedy based on marijuana themes; Cheech and Chong’s Up in Smoke (1978) set the template. Comedy Terms That Every Actor Should Know: Comedy in general asks actors for timing ('most comedy has clean beats'; 'with comedy, pick up your cues'). It’s about comedy as a whole, not stoner comedy.
stoner_comedy.how: neither of its sources read directly, both from search summaries, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: genre-wide: Inherited from comedy: the genre is comedy by definition and actor-training trade press treats timing as what comedy asks of actors. No stoner-specific source states it, so confidence stays low.

stoner_comedy.uncertainty: The definition rests on Wikipedia, and the source on comic timing is a search summary of Backstage about comedy generally (the page couldn’t be opened). Improvisation is documented for Cheech and Chong only, so the research didn’t name it. It holds for the whole genre only by definition, and no source states a technical convention, so it stays at low confidence.

superhero.claim: Superhero roles ask for intensive physical training and learned fight choreography.
superhero.source: Deseret News, 'Superhero stunts demand a blend of fighting styles', https://www.deseret.com/2012/5/1/20410141/superhero-stunts-demand-a-blend-of-fighting-styles/; InsideHook, 'The Fitness Regimens 7 Actors Used to Get Into Superhero Shape', https://www.insidehook.com/wellness/how-to-get-into-superhero-shape
superhero.sourceSupports: From search summaries: actors spent months learning the body mechanics of martial arts before fight sequences were built around them; Johansson describes choreographed steps 'to make it safe'; Larson’s training combined lifting with fight-choreography sessions.

tags.why: Sources describe months of fight training and choreographed fights as the preparation the roles demanded.

superhero.uncertainty: These are search summaries only. Green-screen work, also likely, isn’t one of the requirements the game can ask for, and wasn’t sourced here.

supernatural.claim: No source was found that establishes an acting demand specific to supernatural films.
supernatural.source: The Hollywood Reporter, 'Ghostbusters: How the Visual Effects Team Brought Slimer...', https://hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-news/ghostbusters-how-visual-effects-team-911727/amp
supernatural.sourceSupports: From a search summary: the production used actresses on set as ghosts so the cast could react to them rather than to a tennis ball.
supernatural.uncertainty: This is one production, and an article about effects. Reacting to unseen presences isn’t one of the requirements the game can ask for.

surrealist.claim: Buñuel, the defining surrealist filmmaker, told actors as little as possible and directed them mostly through physical movement and outward gesture.
surrealist.sourceSupports: From a search summary: 'Buñuel told actors as little as possible, and limited his directions mostly to physical movements'; another result notes control of actors 'with special attention paid to gesture and outward appearance'.
surrealist.uncertainty: One director stands in for the movement. The source supports an approach that isn’t psychological, but it doesn’t fit any of the requirements the game can ask for.

survival.claim: Survival films can rest on a single actor with almost no dialogue; All Is Lost has one actor and about 51 words.
survival.sourceSupports: From a search summary: no other actors in the film and very few lines of dialogue (51 words). A review site describes DiCaprio in The Revenant conveying pain 'through grunts, moans, and sheer bodily exertion'.
survival.uncertainty: Two films stand in for the genre. Physical endurance is implied, but no credible source documents it as something asked of actors. The genre’s definition, physical survival, doesn’t on its own call for stunt work, so the research didn’t name Fights And Stunts.

sword_and_sandal.claim: Italian pepla cast bodybuilders, led by Steve Reeves, as their heroes.
sword_and_sandal.source: Wikipedia, 'Steve Reeves', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Reeves (pointer); The Film Magazine, 'A Journey Into Italian Peplum (c.1958-1965)', https://www.thefilmagazine.com/italian-peplum-c-1958-1965/
sword_and_sandal.sourceSupports: From search summaries: Reeves, a former Mr. Universe, made 14 pepla from 1957 to 1964, and many bodybuilders followed him to Italy to play Herculean leads.
sword_and_sandal.uncertainty: The sources support a casting convention (physique), which isn’t one of the requirements the game can ask for. Sword combat and declamatory delivery weren’t sourced.

sword_and_sorcery.claim: The genre’s defining film had its lead train in heavy broadsword fighting, falls and riding.
sword_and_sorcery.source: Wikipedia, 'Conan the Barbarian (1982 film)', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conan_the_Barbarian_(1982_film) (pointer); Yardbarker, 'Arnold Schwarzenegger Recalls Hours of Training With a Japanese Swordsman', https://www.yardbarker.com/general_sports/articles/arnold_schwarzenegger_recalls_hours_of_training_with_a_japanese_swordsman_to_perfect_conan_the_barbarian/s1_17782_43964330
sword_and_sorcery.sourceSupports: From search summaries: Schwarzenegger trained with an 11-pound broadsword two hours a day for three months under swordmaster Kiyoshi Yamazaki, plus weapons, martial-arts and riding training, and learned to fall, roll and jump from fifteen feet.

tags.why: Its touchstone film took months of sword training and falls, and the genre’s definition itself centers on sword-wielding heroes in violent adventures.

sword_and_sorcery.uncertainty: It’s one film. Heightened mythic delivery wasn’t sourced.

techno_thriller.claim: No source was found on delivering technical jargon. One techno-thriller series had its cast attend hacking seminars and its lead learn to type code on camera.
techno_thriller.source: Engadget, 'Mr. Robot has an FBI consultant to make hacking look authentic', https://www.engadget.com/2016-03-14-mr-robot-sxsw-interview.html
techno_thriller.sourceSupports: From search summaries: the cast and creator attended hacking seminars; Malek had a typing instructor and typed parts of real code as the camera rolled.
techno_thriller.uncertainty: It’s one series, and technical credibility isn’t one of the requirements the game can ask for.

teen.claim: Teen films and series often cast actors in their twenties or older as high-school characters.
teen.source: IndieWire, 'Adult Actors Playing Teenagers', https://www.indiewire.com/gallery/adult-actors-playing-teenagers/; TV Tropes, 'Dawson Casting' (pointer)
teen.sourceSupports: Search summaries list examples (Grease, Clueless, Dawson’s Creek, Gossip Girl) of adults playing teenagers.
teen.uncertainty: This is a casting convention, not a skill, and it isn’t one of the requirements the game can ask for. No source was found on adolescent behavior as a skill.

thriller.claim: No source was found on thriller acting. The sources describe tension built by editing, close-ups, silence and pacing.
thriller.sourceSupports: From a search summary: tension 'is created by delaying what the audience sees as inevitable' through menacing situations. It says nothing on performance.
thriller.uncertainty: There’s no acting source. Restraint under pressure is a reasonable reading but is unsourced.

time_travel.claim: In Looper, playing a younger version of Bruce Willis’s character took three hours of prosthetics daily and study of recordings of Willis’s lines and his films. That is one production, not a time-travel convention.
time_travel.source: Craig Elvy and Tom Russell, How Looper Made Joseph Gordon-Levitt Look (& Sound) Like Bruce Willis (Screen Rant, 2024), https://screenrant.com/looper-joseph-gordon-levitt-bruce-willis-face-effects/ [read directly]; The Hollywood Reporter, Looper: Joseph Gordon-Levitt Talks Physical Transformation (The Hollywood Reporter), https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-news/dark-knight-joseph-gordon-levitt-looper-rian-johnson-bruce-willis-311133/ [from a search summary]
time_travel.sourceSupports: How Looper Made Joseph Gordon-Levitt Look (& Sound) Like Bruce Willis: A 3-hour daily makeup application (lip pieces, nose, eyebrows, contacts); 'Willis made recordings of younger Joe’s lines so Gordon-Levitt could match his tone and inflection.' Looper: Joseph Gordon-Levitt Talks Physical Transformation: It led to a paywall and wasn’t read; only its title was.
time_travel.how: one of its two sources read directly and the other from a search summary, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: subgenre-or-role: The demand belongs to the role of a character’s past or future self played by a different actor. Many time-travel films have no such role, or handle it by casting or de-aging; no credible source states it as a genre convention (only TV Tropes and listicles).

time_travel.uncertainty: Searches turned up only trope wikis and listicles on characters meeting younger or older selves. De-aging effects (Tron: Legacy, for one) can replace the actor’s transformation entirely.
time_travel.belongsTo: roles playing another actor’s character at a different age, a past or future self

tragedy.claim: Classical tragedy is enacted in language 'enriched with ornaments' (Aristotle); Greek tragic actors wore masks and the choral parts were sung.
tragedy.source: Wikipedia, 'Tragedy', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tragedy (pointer, quoting Aristotle's Poetics); Almeida Theatre, 'Greek Theatre: At A Glance', https://almeida.co.uk/get-involved/resource-hub/greek-theatre-at-a-glance/
tragedy.sourceSupports: Wikipedia: Aristotle defines tragedy as enacted 'by means of language enriched [with ornaments]'; 'All actors were male and wore masks'; choral parts were sung. Almeida: masks 'allowing actors to play multiple roles' with exaggerated features read from a distance; tragic actors wore raised boots.

tags.why: Aristotle’s definition makes ornamented, heightened language part of what tragedy is.
Almeida and Wikipedia both state that Greek tragic actors performed in masks, often playing several roles.

tragedy.uncertainty: Both hold for classical tragedy, Greek and in verse, not for modern prose or film tragedy. Almeida’s page didn’t mention verse when read; that came from Wikipedia’s account of Aristotle. On review (October 10, 2026), applying them to every tragedy would have asked Heightened Language of Woyzeck, Miss Julie and Riders To The Sea, so they aren’t requirements of the whole genre.
tragedy.belongsTo: classical verse tragedy, where a play asks for them itself (Macbeth calls for Classical Text most of all)

true_crime.claim: Dramatized true crime casts actors as real people, and acting coaches treat matching a real person’s speech, including accent where it differs, as one important part of preparing such a role, alongside voice quality and physicality. Accent isn’t required when the person’s speech is close to the actor’s, and much true crime is documentary with no actors at all.
true_crime.source: Alexander Lee-Rekers, Playing a Real-Life Person as an Actor (StageMilk, 2022), https://www.stagemilk.com/playing-a-real-life-person-as-an-actor/ [read directly]; Boing Boing (on WIRED's 'Technique Critique' with dialect coach Erik Singer), A movie accent expert comments on 31 actors playing real people (Boing Boing, 2017), https://boingboing.net/2017/08/23/a-movie-accent-comments-on-31.html [from a search summary]
true_crime.sourceSupports: Playing a Real-Life Person as an Actor: "A lot of actors will jump straight to accent, and that is an important part of the process! But it’s not the only thing to consider." It recommends researching how the person actually spoke and moved, and doesn’t say an accent is always required. It’s about real-person roles generally, not true crime. A movie accent expert comments on 31 actors playing real people: From a search summary: a dialect coach reviews accent work by actors playing real people. It shows accent work is a recurring part of real-person roles, and says nothing about true crime as a genre.
true_crime.how: one of its two sources read directly and the other from a search summary, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: subgenre-or-role: The demand comes from the role type (portraying a real person whose speech differs from the actor’s), which is found in biopics and historical drama as much as in true crime, and it doesn’t arise in documentary true crime or when the person sounds like the actor. No source ties accent to true crime as a genre.

true_crime.uncertainty: StageMilk is an actor-training site, credible for practice but not a reference work. No trade or scholarly source on acting in dramatized true crime was found. That much true crime is documentary is common knowledge, not sourced here.
true_crime.belongsTo: roles in dramatized true crime that portray real people whose speech differs from the actor’s own

vampire.claim: Actors in vampire roles may have to learn to speak clearly in prosthetic fangs; several notable Draculas wore none.
vampire.sourceSupports: From a search summary: prosthetic fangs make some sounds hard to pronounce; Juliet Landau wore hers for a long period before playing Drusilla to learn to speak with them; Langella and Lugosi wore no fangs as Dracula.
vampire.uncertainty: TV Tropes isn’t credible enough to support a requirement. The Stan Winston School page on Interview with the Vampire showed no text when opened. Fang work is minor prosthetics, not heavy Physical Transformation.

war.claim: War films routinely put casts through military boot camps run by advisers so they can play soldiers credibly.
