war.source: Military.com, 'Meet the Man Who Puts Movie Stars Through Boot Camp', https://www.military.com/podcasts/left-of-boom/2021/02/16/dale-dyes-movie-stars-boot-camp.html; Coffee or Die, 'These Acclaimed War Movies Took Realistic Preparation to Extreme Levels', https://www.coffeeordie.com/article/platoon-movie-boot-camps
war.sourceSupports: From search summaries: Dale Dye ran a 30-day military-style boot camp for the Platoon cast and an intensive one for Saving Private Ryan (sleeping in rain, 5-mile runs); his company Warriors Inc. trains actors for war films.

tags.why: The sources document sustained military physical training for combat roles as standard preparation.

war.uncertainty: None of the requirements the game can ask for is exactly military drill and bearing; Fights And Stunts covers only the physical-action part. These are search summaries.

western.claim: Western productions run 'cowboy camps' that teach actors horse riding and gun handling.
western.source: CinemaBlend, 'I Thought Yellowstone's Cowboy Camp Was About Learning To Rope And Ride...', https://www.cinemablend.com/interviews/i-thought-yellowstone-cowboy-camp-learning-rope-ride-marshals-star-schooled-me-what-actors-really-need-know; Netflix Tudum, 'Ransom Canyon cast cowboy boot camp', https://www.netflix.com/tudum/videos/ransom-canyon-behind-the-scenes-cowboy-boot-camp
western.sourceSupports: From search summaries: camps teach riding, mounting and dismounting, roping and firearm handling; Tim Blake Nelson trained with guns for about five months for gun tricks in The Ballad of Buster Scruggs.

tags.why: Riding and gun handling are trained physical-action skills the sources show westerns requiring; firearms handling falls within stage-combat training.

western.uncertainty: The examples are mostly recent TV westerns. Horsemanship isn’t stage combat, so Fights And Stunts fits only part of it. Laconic manner wasn’t sourced.

whodunit.claim: For Murder on the Orient Express (2017), Kenneth Branagh worked with a dialect coach three times a week and listened to recordings of 27 Belgian accents to play Poirot. The accent belongs to that detective role, not to the whodunit form.
whodunit.source: Agatha Christie Ltd (no byline), 9 Preparatory Steps Branagh Took To Play Hercule Poirot (agathachristie.com, 2017), https://www.agathachristie.com/film-and-tv/murder-on-the-orient-express/9-preparatory-steps-branagh-took-to-play-hercule-poirot [read directly]
whodunit.sourceSupports: 9 Preparatory Steps Branagh Took To Play Hercule Poirot: 'He met with a dialect coach three times a week to study and practice Poirot’s accent'; he 'listened to recordings of 27 different Belgian accents'; he began learning French 'after Wallonian dialect defeated him'.
whodunit.how: its one source read directly, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: subgenre-or-role: One production, one role. The demand comes from the character (a Belgian detective played by an English-speaking actor), not from the whodunit structure; many whodunits have no accented lead.

whodunit.uncertainty: The source is the rights-holder’s promotional site, reliable for the facts but about one film. Ensemble suspect-playing wasn’t sourced.

yakuza.claim: The 1960s ninkyo (chivalry) yakuza film formulaically climaxed in the hero’s katana showdown against a rival gang. The 1970s jitsuroku cycle replaced it with chaotic, unheroic brawls and gunplay. Sources describe the fights, not actors’ training.
yakuza.source: David Hanley, Tradition and Modernity in Japanese Yakuza Films of the 1960s and 70s (Offscreen, 2011), https://offscreen.com/view/japanese_yakuza_films [read directly]; David Wilentz, Yakuza Films at the Asia Society (The Brooklyn Rail, 2008), https://brooklynrail.org/2008/03/film/yakuza-films-at-the-asia-society/ [read directly]; Jasper Sharp, 10 great Japanese gangster films (BFI, 2013), https://www.bfi.org.uk/lists/10-great-japanese-gangster-films [read directly]
yakuza.sourceSupports: Tradition and Modernity in Japanese Yakuza Films of the 1960s and 70s: Ninkyo climaxes feature 'the hero armed only with a traditional katana sword slicing his way through a gang of bad yakuza with guns'; in Battles Without Honor and Humanity yakuza’s 'hands shake when they fire a gun'; 'a free-for-all brawl, with Tetsuya Watari fighting in a downpour'. Yakuza Films at the Asia Society: 1960s yakuza films were 'always climaxing in a showdown where the anti-hero takes down all nemeses with a katana', 'a bloody ballet of sword swinging'. 10 great Japanese gangster films: Ken Takakura as 'the stoic, tattooed, katana-wielding tough guy'; Fukasaku’s jitsuroku style 'stripped away the mythos and surface sheen of the old-school ninkyo eiga of the 1960s'.
yakuza.how: all three of its sources read directly, reviewed October 10, 2026

tags.why: subgenre-or-role: Two independent critics state the climactic sword fight as a formula of the ninkyo cycle, so the demand is supported for that subgenre and its leads. No source states fight work as a convention of yakuza film overall; jitsuroku and later films are described by violence and gunplay, not choreographed combat.

yakuza.uncertainty: The sources are film criticism about screen content, not about what actors trained for. A whole-genre combat demand might be argued from violence across cycles, but no source says it, and much later yakuza cinema (Kitano’s, for one) isn’t led by fight choreography.
yakuza.belongsTo: the lead’s climactic sword fight in ninkyo eiga, the chivalry yakuza films of the 1960s

action.claim: The action genre is defined by fights, chases, shootouts and stunt work.
action.sourceSupports: 'Action film is a film genre that predominantly features chase sequences, fights, shootouts, explosions, and stunt work.' Actor preparation isn’t discussed.

tags.why: The definition names fights and stunt work as what the genre predominantly features.

action.uncertainty: Wikipedia was used only as a lead. Stunt work is often done by doubles, so the page doesn’t say the actor does it.

action_comedy.claim: Action comedy combines action with humor that plays a central role, descended from silent comedians’ chases, gags and stunts.
action_comedy.sourceSupports: Read through an automatic summary of the page: humor 'plays a relatively central role'; silent comedians such as Chaplin and Keaton featured 'chases, gags and stunts'. The earlier quoted phrase 'relies on the characters to bring out the humor' didn’t come back in this reading.

tags.why: The genre is action plus comedy; the page links its roots to chases and stunts.
Humor 'plays a relatively central role' by definition.

action_comedy.uncertainty: The page was read through an automatic summary, and its remarks on Jackie Chan may be the summary’s own, so the research didn’t name Physical Comedy.

backstage_musical.claim: In a backstage musical the story stops for diegetic performance numbers in a show being produced.
backstage_musical.sourceSupports: 'The film’s narrative trajectory often comes to a halt one or more times to allow a performance'; the songs are 'diegetic numbers'; plots revolve around 'the production of a play or musical revue'; Busby Berkeley typified the genre.

tags.why: Performance numbers with songs are the genre’s defining feature.
The plots stage musical revues and the genre is typified by Busby Berkeley’s production numbers.

backstage_musical.uncertainty: The page names 'songs' and 'performances' explicitly; dance follows from 'musical revue' and Berkeley rather than from an explicit sentence about dancing.

comedy.claim: Comic timing, the use of pauses, cadence, delivery and pacing to land a joke, is the core comic skill.
comedy.sourceSupports: From a search summary: 'Comedic timing is the use of pauses, cadence, delivery, and pacing to land a joke.'

tags.why: The source defines comic timing as the craft comedy rests on.

comedy.uncertainty: MasterClass’s page couldn’t be opened; the definition came back in a search. The 'listening to scene partners' part of the earlier claim wasn’t confirmed again.

docufiction.claim: Docufiction’s main characters are often non-professionals essentially playing themselves, unscripted, with improvised dialogue and genuine reactions.
docufiction.sourceSupports: 'The main character or characters—often portrayed by non-professional or amateur actors—are essentially playing themselves'; docufictions 'are usually not scripted' and use participants’ 'own genuine reactions and their own improvisational dialogue'.

tags.why: The page says docufictions are usually unscripted, with improvisational dialogue.
Participants portray 'their own genuine reactions' on camera, which is naturalistic on-camera behavior as a convention.

docufiction.uncertainty: The participants are often not actors at all, so what it asks of an actor applies loosely.

farce.claim: Farce calls for highly stylized performances and dramatic reactions, with adept comic timing for wordplay, visual gags and slapstick.
farce.sourceSupports: 'broad, larger-than-life characters, often calling for highly stylized performances and dramatic reactions'; 'There may be wordplay, visual gags and slapstick, requiring the need for adept comic timing by the actors.'

tags.why: The page names comic timing as something the form needs: 'requiring the need for adept comic timing by the actors'.
Visual gags and slapstick are named conventions of the form.

farce.uncertainty: 'Highly stylized performances' is about physical and emotional style, not language, so the research didn’t name Heightened Language.

found_footage.claim: Found-footage films routinely use improvisation and naturalistic acting, and the actors may shoot the film themselves as they perform.
found_footage.sourceSupports: 'the cinematography may be done by the actors themselves as they perform'; 'shaky camera work, improvisation and naturalistic acting are routinely employed'.

tags.why: The page says improvisation is 'routinely employed'.
Naturalistic acting is 'routinely employed', the page says, and actors may operate the camera.

found_footage.uncertainty: Wikipedia was used only as a lead.

jidaigeki.claim: Jidaigeki uses a contrived, formal, archaic register of Japanese speech, stock makeup and catchphrases, and stylized sword fights.
jidaigeki.sourceSupports: 'A contrived form of old-fashioned Japanese speech, using modern pronunciation and grammar with a high degree of formality and frequent archaisms'; heroes wear eye makeup; protagonists deliver set catchphrases (kimarizerifu); sword fights follow set conventions, and chambara films use stylized violence.

tags.why: The page describes a formal, archaic stylized speech register as a convention.
Sword fights are a standing convention; chambara is the sword-fighting branch.

jidaigeki.uncertainty: The page was read through an automatic summary. It doesn’t say how much of the swordplay the lead actors do themselves.

kaiju.claim: Japanese kaiju films used suit actors performing inside stiff latex or rubber creature suits on miniature sets.
kaiju.sourceSupports: Tsuburaya 'decided to attempt to create suits, called creature suits, for a human (suit actor) to wear and act in'; 'Due to the extreme stiffness of the latex or rubber suits, filming would often be done at double speed'; combined with miniature city sets.

tags.why: Suit actors perform as the creature inside full creature suits.

kaiju.uncertainty: Physical Transformation fits suit actors, not the human cast. Reacting to unseen threats wasn’t sourced in this reading. On review (October 10, 2026), a demand on suit actors alone wasn’t enough to make it a requirement of the whole genre.
kaiju.belongsTo: the suit actor playing the creature

martial_arts.claim: Martial-arts roles are often played by real martial artists; otherwise actors train for the role, helped by doubles, wire work and camera tricks.
martial_arts.sourceSupports: 'these roles are often played by actors who are real martial artists. If not, actors frequently train in preparation for their roles or the action director may rely more on stylized action or film making tricks'; techniques include 'doubles, undercranking, wire work'.

tags.why: Real martial-arts skill or role-specific fight training is stated as the norm.

martial_arts.uncertainty: Wikipedia was used only as a lead.

melodrama.claim: Film melodrama uses exaggerated staging, score and performance; characters wear their hearts on their sleeves.
melodrama.source: BFI, 'Too Much: Melodrama on Film', https://www.bfi.org.uk/too-much
melodrama.sourceSupports: Melodrama 'employs exaggerated staging, score and performance to create the ultimate spectacle'; 'a passionate purge of emotion'; 'heightened dramatics'; characters 'rarely behave rationally'.
melodrama.uncertainty: The source supports exaggerated emotional performance, but Heightened Language means heightened or stylized language, which the BFI doesn’t mention. None of the requirements the game can ask for fits, and none was forced.

mockumentary.claim: Mockumentaries can be partly or wholly improvised and are presented through documentary devices such as talking heads and cinéma vérité.
mockumentary.sourceSupports: 'Mockumentaries can be partly or wholly improvised'; 'often presented as historical documentaries, with B roll and talking heads ... or as cinéma vérité pieces'.

tags.why: The page states mockumentaries can be partly or wholly improvised.

mockumentary.uncertainty: Deadpan naturalism wasn’t stated outright, so the research didn’t name Naturalism On Camera. The page didn’t establish that mockumentaries are always comic, so it didn’t name Comic Timing either.

mumblecore.claim: Naturalism in performance and dialogue is a key feature of almost all mumblecore; early films used non-professionals and some used prominent improvisation.
mumblecore.sourceSupports: 'Naturalism – both in performance and dialogue – is a key feature of almost all mumblecore films'; 'Early mumblecore films tended to feature non-professional actors'; 'Some mumblecore films feature a prominent use of improvisation, with the cast sharing script credits'; Bujalski’s are 'mostly scripted'.

tags.why: Naturalistic performance is called a key feature of almost all mumblecore films.

mumblecore.uncertainty: Improvisation is in 'some' films, not all; the page notes exceptions that are mostly scripted. The review of October 10, 2026 took Improvisation away for that reason: the convention is the naturalism, Naturalism On Camera.

musical.claim: A musical film integrates musical numbers into the plot; characters sing and dance.
musical.sourceSupports: From a search summary: a musical film 'integrates musical numbers within the plot'; characters often sing and dance to express emotion and advance the plot.

tags.why: Britannica says musical numbers are integrated in the plot, and characters sing.
Britannica, in a search summary, says characters sing and dance.

musical.uncertainty: Britannica’s pages couldn’t be opened; the search summary may blend Britannica with other results, especially the sentence about singing and dancing.

nature_documentary.claim: Nature documentaries almost all have a human presenter, whose role ranges from explanatory voice-over to on-camera interaction with animals.
nature_documentary.sourceSupports: 'Almost all have a human presenter, the role varies widely, ranging from explanatory voice-overs to extensive interaction or even confrontation with animals.'

tags.why: Explanatory voice-over is named as a standard presenter role.

nature_documentary.uncertainty: Presenting isn’t acting in the usual sense, and presenting on camera isn’t exactly one of the requirements the game can ask for.

neorealism.claim: Italian neorealism was filmed on location among the poor and working class, frequently with non-professional actors.
neorealism.source: Wikipedia, 'Italian neorealism', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_neorealism (pointer); previously cited: Britannica, 'Neorealism', https://www.britannica.com/art/Neorealism-Italian-art (not reachable)
neorealism.sourceSupports: A search summary of Wikipedia: 'a style of film characterized by stories set amongst the poor and working class, filmed on location, frequently using nonprofessional actors'; where known actors were cast they played 'strongly against their normal character types'.

tags.why: Non-professionals playing ordinary people on location is the movement’s defining convention, which implies unadorned on-camera naturalism.

neorealism.uncertainty: The Britannica page couldn’t be opened, and searches returned Wikipedia and others instead. Naturalism On Camera is inferred from casting and location practice; no source here states a performance style in so many words. On review (October 10, 2026), an inference wasn’t enough to make it a requirement of the whole genre.
neorealism.belongsTo: non-professional casting, a choice of who’s cast rather than a technique asked of an actor

new_wave.claim: The New Wave promoted a naturalistic style with location shooting, improvised dialogue and natural light.
new_wave.sourceSupports: Search summary attributed to Britannica: 'The New Wave movement promoted a more naturalistic filmmaking style, with location shoots, improvised dialogue, and natural lighting.'

tags.why: Improvised dialogue is named as a convention.
The movement is described as promoting a naturalistic style.

new_wave.uncertainty: The Britannica page couldn’t be opened, and the search didn’t return the New Wave page itself, so the attribution is unconfirmed, and this is secondhand.

period_drama.claim: Period dramas employ historical advisers who teach actors how to speak, stand, sit, eat and gesture in the manner of the era.
period_drama.source: Detroit News, 'PBS special examines the etiquette of Downton Abbey', https://eu.detroitnews.com/story/entertainment/television/2015/01/04/downton-abbey-pbs-special/21210235/; PBS, 'The Manners of Downton Abbey', https://cm-pressroom.pbs.org/programs/m/manners-of-downton-abbey; previously cited: DataCalculus, 'Dialect coaching for actors in period pieces'
period_drama.sourceSupports: From search summaries: Alastair Bruce advised Downton Abbey actors 'on how to speak, stand, sit, eat, drink, dress', posture and 'the use of vocabulary'; Lily James: 'The main thing I had to learn was posture'. DataCalculus (read directly) says dialect coaches evoke 'the culture, education, and social class of the period'.
period_drama.uncertainty: The earlier source, DataCalculus, is a data-analytics company’s blog and too weak to support a requirement, so the research didn’t name Accents. The Downton evidence is one series. The review of October 10, 2026 took Heightened Language away: it’s verse and rhetoric, and the research is about period speech, bearing and manners in one series, which it doesn’t fit.

romantic_comedy.claim: Under the Hays Code, romantic comedies relied on verbal sparring and physical comedy.
romantic_comedy.sourceSupports: From a search summary: the Hays Code 'prohibited explicit mention of sexual relationships, leading to films' relying on verbal sparring and physical comedy instead'; the genre is defined by the lighthearted pursuit of love.

tags.why: The genre is comedy, and Britannica names verbal sparring as a defining resource.

romantic_comedy.uncertainty: Britannica couldn’t be opened. Physical comedy is tied to the Hays-era films, so the research didn’t name Physical Comedy for the genre as a whole. Chemistry isn’t one of the requirements the game can ask for.

samurai.claim: Samurai films use tate, a stage swordplay of fixed forms that actors memorize and combine, with strict posture and etiquette.
samurai.source: The Gate (thegate12.com), article on tate, https://thegate12.com/article/283
samurai.sourceSupports: Tate is 'stage fighting in brawls or with swords, in stage plays and movies' using fixed forms actors memorize and combine; it requires straight back and planted heels, proper kimono wear and sword etiquette.

tags.why: The page describes learned, choreographed stage swordplay for film and stage.

samurai.uncertainty: The Gate is a Japan-culture travel site describing a tate experience, not an academic source. Period bearing isn’t exactly one of the requirements the game can ask for.

screwball_comedy.claim: Screwball comedy is built on fast-paced, overlapping repartee combined with slapstick.
screwball_comedy.sourceSupports: 'fast-paced, overlapping repartee'; 'slapstick elements'; Henry Fonda performs 'numerous pratfalls' in The Lady Eve.

tags.why: Fast, overlapping verbal repartee is the genre’s defining feature.
Slapstick elements and pratfalls are named.

screwball_comedy.uncertainty: The page was read through an automatic summary.

sea_adventure.claim: The cited source doesn’t support anything asked of an actor: it’s about nautical literature, whose defining trait is nautical detail and seafaring vernacular.
sea_adventure.sourceSupports: The page discusses 'nautical language' and 'the vernacular expression of seafaring men' in fiction such as Cooper’s The Pilot. It says nothing about film actors or physical work in water.
sea_adventure.uncertainty: This was lowered from medium confidence: the earlier source doesn’t discuss actors at all. Nautical jargon isn’t Heightened Language in the game’s sense. No acting source was found.

silent_film.claim: Silent-film actors conveyed story and emotion through mime, pantomime and exaggerated gesture and expression.
silent_film.sourceSupports: 'Actors in silent films often used techniques of mime and pantomime to convey emotions and actions, making performances highly expressive and physical'; 'exaggerated expressions and gestures'.
silent_film.uncertainty: None of the requirements the game can ask for fits wordless pantomime: Physical Comedy means slapstick and clowning, and silent drama isn’t comic. The gap is in the game’s requirements, not in the evidence. StudioBinder is a production-software blog.

social_realism.claim: Ken Loach, the touchstone of British social realism, casts non-professionals alongside actors, withholds the full script, shoots in sequence and encourages improvisation.
social_realism.source: No Film School, 'Ten Directing Lessons Inspired by Ken Loach', https://nofilmschool.com/directed-by-ken-loach; Into Film, 'Ken Loach, social realism...', https://www.intofilm.org/news-and-views/articles/ken-loach-feature
social_realism.sourceSupports: From search summaries: Loach uses non-professionals, limits actors’ access to the script, shoots chronologically, 'avoids extensive rehearsals and encourages actors to improvise as a way of achieving spontaneity'.

tags.why: Loach encourages actors to improvise for spontaneity.
The method aims at spontaneous, naturalistic on-camera behavior.

social_realism.uncertainty: The Into Film page showed no text when opened. One director’s method stands in for the genre. On review (October 10, 2026), one director’s method wasn’t enough to make it a requirement of the whole genre.
social_realism.belongsTo: Ken Loach’s productions and those that work his way

swashbuckler.claim: Fight directors such as Paddy Crean staged swashbuckler swordplay and taught actors sword work for stage and film.
swashbuckler.sourceSupports: Crean ran a London fencing school 'used ... to teach many celebrities sword work for stage and films', often doubled for Errol Flynn, and choreographed films such as The Master of Ballantrae (1953).

tags.why: Staged swordplay taught by a fight director is documented for the genre’s films.

swashbuckler.uncertainty: Crean often doubled Flynn, so some swordplay wasn’t performed by the star.

tokusatsu.claim: Tokusatsu suit actors do their stunts and sword fights inside full costumes that hide their faces, acting through body language, with voices dubbed later.
tokusatsu.sourceSupports: 'the suit actor does all of their stunts while in a full costume that normally obscures their identity'; roles 'may require extensive sword fights, actions and stunts within a physically restrictive environment'; 'extensive body language and pantomime are crucial'; 'the actor’s voice is dubbed during after-recording'.

tags.why: Suit actors do stunts and sword fights in costume.
Full-costume performance with the face hidden, conveyed through body language.

tokusatsu.uncertainty: It applies to suit actors, not the unmasked cast. Voice dubbing is done to the suit actor, not by them, so the research didn’t name Voice-Led Performance. On review (October 10, 2026), a demand on suit actors alone wasn’t enough to make it a requirement of the whole genre.

tragicomedy.claim: Tragicomedy holds tragic and comic elements side by side, with tone shifting between serious and comic, often within a scene.
tragicomedy.sourceSupports: From search summaries: tragicomedies 'hold comedy and tragedy side by side in balance'; the tone 'shifts between serious and comic, often within the same scene'. A Semantic Scholar paper notes Chekhov asked the Moscow Art Theatre for 'a lighter touch'.

tags.why: By definition the form contains comedy the actor must play alongside tragic stakes.

tragicomedy.uncertainty: These are genre guides, not acting sources. The requirement comes from the definition.

werewolf.claim: Werewolf roles can require long prosthetic transformations that the actor must perform through.
werewolf.source: The Hollywood Reporter, 'Wolf Man Star Christopher Abbott Talks His 7-Hour Transformation', https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-features/wolf-man-star-christopher-abbott-1236109770/; IndieWire, 'Wolf Man: Christopher Abbott Needed 650 Prosthetic Pieces', https://www.indiewire.com/features/craft/wolf-man-christopher-abbott-650-prosthetic-pieces-interview-1235085626/
werewolf.sourceSupports: From search summaries: the final transformation stage took up to seven hours; Abbott called it 'tedious and arduous' and practiced lines in a mirror to see 'how your face moves underneath the prosthetics'.

tags.why: Heavy multi-stage prosthetic transformation the actor performs through.

werewolf.uncertainty: It’s one film; earlier werewolf films vary, and some used CGI. On review (October 10, 2026), one film’s prosthetic transformation wasn’t enough to make it a requirement of the whole genre.
werewolf.belongsTo: the werewolf role in practical-effects productions

wuxia.claim: Wuxia films by King Hu and the Shaw Brothers used wire- and trampoline-assisted acrobatics and choreographed sword action.
wuxia.source: Wikipedia, 'Wuxia', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wuxia (pointer); Wikipedia, 'Wire fu' (from a search summary only)
wuxia.sourceSupports: 'sophisticated action choreography using wire and trampoline assisted acrobatics combined with sped-up camera techniques'; Yuen Woo-ping became famous as a wuxia action choreographer.

tags.why: Choreographed, wire-assisted acrobatic fight action is a defining convention.

wuxia.uncertainty: The page doesn’t say how much the actors perform themselves rather than doubles.

zombie.claim: Zombie productions train performers to move consistently as the undead, taught by the stunt team.
zombie.source: TheWrap, 'Army of the Dead: Zack Snyder Sent Hundreds of Extras to Zombie School', https://www.thewrap.com/army-of-the-dead-zack-snyder-extras-zombie-school/
zombie.sourceSupports: From a search summary: about 200 extras attended 'Zombie School', where the stunt team taught them 'how to move and act like a zombie'. Walking Dead extras also attended a zombie school (Collider).

tags.why: Trained creature movement for undead roles, under makeup.

zombie.uncertainty: It applies to the undead performers, largely extras, not the living leads. Survival physicality for the living cast wasn’t sourced. On review (October 10, 2026), a demand on the undead performers alone wasn’t enough to make it a requirement of the whole genre.
